Policy : Claim × Evidence × Context → Assessment | REJECTED as the TYPE — this is the signature

governance.anchor: Policy is an INDEPENDENT NORMATIVE OBJECT. All ten alternative placements are refuted above. It is not part of K, P, T, evidence, authority, governance, history, or Σ, and it is not mere configuration. This is a conclusion by elimination, and the elimination is complete over the mandate's own list.

rationale_evidence.anchor: The decisive discrimination: a policy is an OBJECT that is applied, not a function that is called. It has identity, a version, an applicability window, and it can be composed and compared. A bare function has none of those. ... versioning is only meaningful for an object.
rationale_evidence.statement: Decisive discrimination for Policy's category: a Policy is an OBJECT that is applied (having identity, version, an applicability window, and composability/comparability), not a bare function that is called — versioning (corpus-named 'Migration-Policy v3', 'ChangePolicy v3') is only meaningful for an object.

rationale_evidence.anchor: codomain {True, False, Unknown} — three-valued ... totality partial — undefined outside ValidityInterval ... composability ∧ only — meet-semilattice; ∨ REFUTED ... identity (id, version); version is semantically load-bearing ... executed: same id, different ResolutionBehavior, different result ... p
rationale_evidence.statement: Per-property analysis of Policy: three-valued codomain, partial totality (undefined outside its validity interval), deterministic given fixed gates, composable only under conjunction (a meet-semilattice; disjunction is REFUTED as a composition operator), four distinct equality notions (deferred to a companion artifact 5), identity is (id,version) with version proven semantically load-bearing (same id with different ResolutionBehavior gives a different Apply result), versioning required (corpus names v3 policies), and policy provenance (who authored/authorised it) explicitly recorded as absent from the governing corpus definition (step 57.47) — an unresolved gap.

rationale_evidence.anchor: adm_early(True, None, True, True) → None (Block). A two-valued policy must map Unknown to either True or False silently. The corpus makes that mapping an explicit, named component of the policy object — ResolutionBehavior. ... it connects directly to Σ's Neutral/Unknown — the same epistemic humility
rationale_evidence.statement: Why three-valued semantics matter: an executed example (adm_early with one Unknown gate value producing Block) shows a two-valued policy would have to silently coerce Unknown to True or False, whereas the corpus's ResolutionBehavior makes that coercion an explicit, named, auditable choice — called the single most sophisticated part of the corpus's policy treatment, and noted to be the same epistemic-humility pattern that appears at the Sigma (epistemic status) Neutral/Unknown level, i.e. the same design idea recurring at two levels of the theory.

rationale_evidence.anchor: 8 Policy 'One authoritative current source is sufficient' ... 13 Policy Migration-Policy v3 — named and VERSIONED ... 42 Admissible Pre∧Invariant∧Assurance∧Authorization; no averaging — executed ... 57.47 Policy (Rules, ValidityInterval, ResolutionBehavior) — the canonical type ... 199 Policy = Allo
rationale_evidence.statement: Full step-by-step Policy lineage traced across the corpus (steps 8, 13, 25, 41, 42, 49, 54, 57.47, 86, 91, 104, 127, 139, 199, 202, 206, 207, 240, 252, plus non-step material), each classified by whether it is normative or descriptive, executable, superseded, and whether it survives into the current theory — e.g. step 8's 'one authoritative current source' maps forward into the EKP's single_authoritative rule; step 13 introduces versioned policies (Migration-Policy v3), establishing that version is part of identity; step 199's 'Policy = Allowed' and step 207's self-contradictory 'Policy = Decision' / 'Policy is not a command' are both REFUTED.

rationale_evidence.anchor: Rules (57.47) = the conjunct set of 42.9; ResolutionBehavior (57.47) = the Unknown → Block rule (42.12); ValidityInterval (57.47) = the temporal applicability of 54's 'rule over an applicable context'. Three sources, one object, no invention required. ... 42.9's Assurance conjunct is not a primitive
rationale_evidence.statement: The three separately-sourced Policy fragments (57.47's tuple fields, 42.9's conjunct set, 54's temporal-applicability gloss, 42.12's Unknown-handling rule) are shown to describe the same single object with one substitution needed: 42.9's 'Assurance' conjunct, not being a coherent primitive concept (per the prior-phase Assurance split), maps onto a JustificationStrength >= threshold gate — the Assurance split is shown to survive and sharpen contact with the independently-derived Policy evaluation law, since 'Assurance' as a conjunct was always implicitly a threshold test, never a standalone concept.

rationale_evidence.anchor: Note the pleasing duality with K: (𝕂, merge, ∅) is a join-semilattice — adding knowledge only grows the state. (Policy, ∧) is a meet-semilattice — adding policy only shrinks admissibility. Knowledge accumulates; permission contracts. Neither is an aesthetic choice; both were executed.
rationale_evidence.statement: A structural duality is identified between the two central algebraic objects of the theory: (K, merge, empty) is a join-semilattice (knowledge only accumulates/grows), while (Policy, AND) is a meet-semilattice (permission only contracts) — 'knowledge accumulates; permission contracts', explicitly noted as an executed structural finding, not an aesthetic observation.

rationale_evidence.anchor: frontmatter_present/_parses ✓ structural ... knowledge_id_unique ✓ INVARIANT ... knowledge_id_pattern ✓ POLICY ... enum_values_valid ✓ POLICY ... single_authoritative ✓ GOVERNANCE ... circular_dependency ✓ INVARIANT (mis-typed as warning) ... 3 invariants · 7 policies · 3 governance rules · 3 valida
rationale_evidence.statement: All 18 EKP lint rules are classified against the theory's own categories (descriptive schema, structural constraint, normative policy, validation mechanism, implementation invariant, governance rule), yielding a clean count of 3 invariants, 7 policies, 3 governance rules, 3 validation/structural rules, and 2 descriptive rules, applying the artifact-3 policy/invariant discrimination criterion directly to real running code.

rationale_evidence.anchor: Σ = codomain of Assessment, and Assessment takes Policy. While Policy was undefined, Σ's codomain was undetermined — not unknown, undetermined. ... Same evidence, same assertion, different Σ. Σ is not a property of the assertion — it is a property of the assertion UNDER A POLICY. The mandate's order
rationale_evidence.statement: Explains why Sigma could not have been resolved before Policy: since Sigma is literally the codomain of Assessment, and Assessment takes Policy as an argument, Sigma's codomain was UNDETERMINED (not merely unknown) while Policy remained undefined; the same evidence under different policies producing different Sigma values (Supporting/Weak vs Neutral/None) is direct evidence that Sigma is a property of an assertion UNDER A POLICY, not of the assertion alone — confirming the mandate's Policy-before-Sigma ordering was the correct dependency direction.

rationale_evidence.anchor: EKP implements: identity, referential integrity, typed relations, controlled vocabularies, context, determinism, Σ⊥Γ as declared config, policy representation/interpretation/enforcement/evaluation. EKP does not implement: proposition structure, evidence, temporal validity, provenance, Σ, contradicti
rationale_evidence.statement: Final consolidated engineering-correspondence verdict across the whole programme: the EKP implements identity, referential integrity, typed relations, controlled vocabularies, context, determinism, Sigma-perp-Gamma (as declared config), and policy representation/interpretation/enforcement/evaluation; it does not implement proposition structure, evidence, temporal validity, provenance, Sigma, contradiction, T as a guarded transition, or policy composition; it exceeds the theory with single_authoritative, boundary_consistency, frozen_changed_without_adr, and symmetric related_to; and the theory in turn constrains the implementation by requiring supersedes-acyclicity to be an error over three relation families (supersedes, derived_from, refines), not merely a warning over two.

rationale_evidence.anchor: Governance decision = possibly non-computable input. ... Evidence handling is computable in layers [Retrieve(e), Hash(e), Link(A,e) computable; Assess(e,A) may require a human or statistical model]. ... StatisticalFormula ≠ ComputableKnowledgeOSQuantity ... Probability claims = UNDER-SPECIFIED unles
rationale_evidence.statement: Policy/authority, evidence, statistics and uncertainty are each shown to contain a non-computable normative core: Authorize(actor,action,policy) is decidable only if policy is fully formalized as rules, otherwise it is a possibly non-computable governance-decision input; evidence handling is computable in layers (retrieval/hashing/linkage computable, but Assess(e,A) may require a human or statistical model); a statistical formula's mere existence (e.g. Bayes' rule) does not make a KnowledgeOS quantity computable — a probability claim is UNDER-SPECIFIED without an explicit probability space (Omega,F,P); and Uncertainty is not computable until its semantics are fixed, since a bare number like U(A)=0.2 could mean probability, confidence, epistemic strength, error bound, entropy, or subjective belief — mathematically different things.

rationale_evidence.anchor: Model P1 — Policy as predicate Policy:(K,o)→{true,false} ... Model P2 — Policy as constraint set π={p1,…,pn} Comply(K,o,π)=⋀i pi(K,o) ... Model P3 — Policy as decision procedure Policy(K,o)→PolicyDecision∈{permit,deny,conditional} ... Model P4 — Policy as normative document ... does not automaticall
rationale_evidence.statement: Four candidate Policy models are set out for testing: P1 policy-as-predicate (K,o)->{true,false}; P2 policy-as-constraint-set with conjunctive compliance; P3 policy-as-decision-procedure returning permit/deny/conditional; P4 policy-as-normative-document (textual governance material, not automatically computable) — the last explicitly identified as where the theory becomes blocked.

rationale_evidence.anchor: Assess(A2,default)=(Supporting,Weak) while Assess(A2,strict-provenance)=(Neutral,None). This is a major result. It demonstrates: Σ cannot be derived from the Assertion alone. ... But this does NOT prove that Policy belongs in K. ... K = knowledge content while Policy = conditions governing interpret
rationale_evidence.statement: Re-derives (independently of the parallel Policy-archaeology track) that Sigma cannot be derived from the Assertion alone, using the same policy-dependent Assess(A2,...) example, but explicitly argues this demonstrates Assessment=f(P,E,C,Pi) without proving Pi (or Policy) belongs inside K — K remains knowledge content, Policy remains an external condition governing interpretation/operation.

aliases: Identity, Entity Resolution, Equivalence, Reference Integrity and the Mathematics of Same

sources.note: S0933's Step 38: the identity/entity-resolution/equivalence/reference-integrity foundation, formalizing context-relative denotation, graded identity status, false-merge/false-split asymmetric costs, temporal identity vs state, a multi-level identity hierarchy, the identity graph G_I, semantic (statement) equivalence distinct from entity identity, and cost-sensitive/decision-theoretic/active-learning-based identity resolution. Its own opening presupposes the immediately preceding batch file (S0932, Step 39) as still being Step 37, confirming the Step-39-before-Step-38 file-order deviation.

rows.anchor: If identity is wrong, then Evidence->Claim->Model->Decision can all be mathematically correct about the wrong object. That is one of the most dangerous classes of epistemic failure
rows.statement: Frames identity error as one of the most dangerous epistemic failure classes: correct reasoning about the wrong object.

lineage_claims.quote: We continue from Step 37.

rows.anchor: Identity from Similarity from Equivalence from Reference. They are not interchangeable. Similarity(x,y) does not imply x=y
rows.statement: Distinguishes identity, similarity, equivalence, and reference as non-interchangeable concepts.

rows.anchor: R1 = nexus3.dgverlag.de, R2 = 10.61.133.85, R3 = Nexus repository server, R4 = Nexus OSS 3.69.0 host ... Denotes(R_1)=Denotes(R_2)? That requires evidence. A name is not the entity
rows.statement: Worked four-reference Nexus example illustrating reference-vs-entity denotation requiring evidence.

rows.anchor: denotes:R->E. r_1=r_2 is not required for denotes(r_1)=denotes(r_2). Different references can identify the same entity
rows.statement: Formally defines the denotes function from references to entities.

rows.anchor: server01 in Environment=A and server01 in Environment=B. Name(x)=Name(y) does not imply x=y
rows.statement: Worked counterexample of identical names denoting different entities across environments.

rows.anchor: denotes(r,c) -> e where c is context. This is strongly aligned with DDD. The same linguistic term can have different meanings in different bounded contexts
rows.statement: Extends denotation to be context-relative, aligned with DDD.

rows.anchor: Customer exists in Sales and Billing ... may correspond to the same real-world person or organization, but they are not automatically the same domain object. RealWorldIdentity != DomainObjectIdentity
rows.statement: Worked Customer/Sales/Billing example establishing RealWorldIdentity != DomainObjectIdentity.

rows.anchor: KnowledgeOS must not globally impose GlobalEntityIdentity where the domain has intentionally defined separate identities. Instead Identity is contextual
rows.statement: States one of the most important DDD principles for KnowledgeOS: identity is contextual, not globally imposed.

rows.anchor: entity resolution asks P(SameEntity|r_1,r_2,C). But this immediately introduces uncertainty
rows.statement: Defines entity resolution as a probabilistic inference problem.

rows.anchor: P(SameEntity)=0.97. That does not mean SameEntity=True. It means the evidence supports a high probability under a specified model. This must remain distinct from confirmed identity
rows.statement: Distinguishes probabilistic entity-resolution confidence from confirmed identity.

rows.anchor: IdentityStatus in {Unknown, Candidate, Probable, Confirmed, Rejected, Contextual}. This is much safer than forcing binary identity too early
rows.statement: Defines a six-value graded identity-status taxonomy.

rows.anchor: r_1 and r_2 have matching hostname; IP; service port; environment. We may create CandidateSameEntity(r_1,r_2). But not yet ConfirmedSameEntity
rows.statement: Defines candidate identity as distinct from confirmed identity, worked with a multi-attribute-match example.

rows.anchor: Confirmation might require DNS, CMDB, RuntimeObservation, or HumanConfirmation. The confirmation mechanism becomes provenance
rows.statement: Defines identity-confirmation evidence sources and their provenance role.

rows.anchor: Identity itself becomes an epistemic claim: A: denotes(r_1)=denotes(r_2). Then all Step 32-37 machinery applies: Evidence->Assertion->Validation->Confidence->Decision
rows.statement: States identity is itself an epistemic claim subject to the full evidence/validation/confidence/decision machinery.

rows.anchor: We should therefore reject the idea that identity resolution is merely a database lookup ... when identity is ambiguous IdentityResolution is an epistemic inference problem
rows.statement: Argues identity resolution is often an epistemic inference problem, not merely a database lookup.

rows.anchor: Reflexivity x=x. Symmetry x=y=>y=x. Transitivity x=y and y=z=>x=z. These properties matter
rows.statement: Restates the formal reflexivity/symmetry/transitivity properties of equality.

rows.anchor: Similarity(A,B) and Similarity(B,C). It does not follow that Similarity(A,C). Therefore similarity cannot automatically be treated as equality
rows.statement: States similarity is not necessarily transitive, unlike equality.

rows.anchor: sim(A,B)=0.95, sim(B,C)=0.95 but sim(A,C)=0.60. If we merge A and B, and B and C, we may accidentally merge A and C
rows.statement: Worked counterexample of transitive-closure contamination from thresholded similarity merging.

rows.anchor: A false merge means x!=y but KnowledgeOS stores x=y. Consequences: incorrect evidence aggregation; false conflicts; incorrect history; contaminated statistics; wrong ownership; wrong decisions. This is a high-severity epistemic failure
rows.statement: Defines false merge and its six categories of consequence as a high-severity failure mode.

rows.anchor: The reverse is x=y but KnowledgeOS stores x!=y. Consequences: duplicated knowledge; missed contradictions; fragmented provenance; incorrect counts; duplicated investigations. Both errors matter
rows.statement: Defines false split and its five categories of consequence.

rows.anchor: Cost(FalseMerge) != Cost(FalseSplit). For critical infrastructure, false merging may be significantly more dangerous. Therefore identity thresholds should be domain-specific
rows.statement: States false-merge and false-split costs are asymmetric and domain-specific, requiring domain-specific thresholds.

rows.anchor: Precision = CorrectMerges/AllMerges. Recall = CorrectMerges/AllTrueMatches. A conservative identity policy often prefers high precision
rows.statement: Defines precision/recall for entity resolution and states a conservative policy preference for precision.

rows.anchor: UnknownIdentity should generally remain Unknown rather than being silently merged. This is analogous to our abstention principle
rows.statement: States the conservative identity principle, analogous to the abstention principle.

rows.anchor: P(Same)=0.98. The system should preserve CandidateIdentity unless the domain's threshold allows promotion to Confirmed. This prevents probabilistic inference from silently becoming ontology
rows.statement: States identity confidence must not silently become confirmed identity/ontology.

rows.anchor: A(x) = {name, address, IP, serial, owner, environment, timestamp}. But attributes have different discriminative power
rows.statement: Defines entity-resolution attributes with differing discriminative power.

rows.anchor: UUID or serialNumber highly discriminative. Others are weak: name. IdentityEvidenceStrength(attribute) should vary
rows.statement: Defines identifier-specific evidence strength, distinguishing stable from weak identifiers.

rows.anchor: Even supposedly unique identifiers can fail if systems are misconfigured; identifiers are reused; environments are copied; test data is cloned. UniqueIdentifier should be treated as strong evidence, not metaphysical truth
rows.statement: Warns unique identifiers are strong evidence, not infallible truth, given four collision scenarios.

rows.anchor: Server has IP_t=10.61.133.85 and later IP_{t+1}=10.61.133.90. If IP is treated as identity, the system may incorrectly conclude EntityChanged. The entity may actually be unchanged
rows.statement: Worked IP-change example distinguishing state change from identity change.

rows.anchor: Identity(x) from State(x,t). x_t may represent the state of entity x at time t, without implying a new identity
rows.statement: Formally distinguishes entity identity from time-indexed state.

rows.anchor: hostname_t. Thus Reference(x,t) is time-dependent. This connects directly to Step 16 and Step 17
rows.statement: Extends reference to be time-dependent, connecting to the temporal/bitemporal model (Steps 16-17).

rows.anchor: A_1.0 and A_2.0. Are they SameEntity? Possibly yes at the product level. But SameVersion? clearly no. Therefore identity has levels
rows.statement: Worked software-version example establishing identity has multiple levels (product vs version).

rows.anchor: Product -> ApplicationInstance -> Deployment -> Process. Each can have a distinct identity. Thus IdentityLevel
rows.statement: Defines a four-level identity hierarchy.

rows.anchor: Nexus may refer to: Nexus Repository product; Nexus deployment; Nexus host; Nexus container; Nexus process; Nexus repository; Nexus blob store. These are not interchangeable
rows.statement: Worked seven-sense 'Nexus' example illustrating the identity-level hierarchy.

rows.anchor: EntityType(x). Then EntityType(x) != EntityType(y) can make identity impossible or require an explicit relation
rows.statement: Defines entity type as gating whether identity is even possible between two references.

rows.anchor: Application -> deployedOn -> Server. We should not merge Application with Server. They are related entities
rows.statement: Worked example warning against merging related-but-distinct-type entities.

rows.anchor: An aggregate can define AggregateIdentity. Internal objects may have identities within the aggregate. External systems should interact through the aggregate's defined boundary. KnowledgeOS must respect those boundaries when reconstructing identity
rows.statement: Extends DDD aggregate boundaries into identity reconstruction, requiring KnowledgeOS to respect them.

rows.anchor: Claim -> EntityID. If the entity is deleted or merged, the reference cannot simply disappear. We need ReferenceHistory
rows.statement: Defines referential integrity requiring reference history across entity lifecycle changes.

rows.anchor: x and y are confirmed identical, we can record Merge(x,y,t). But we should not destroy the history
rows.statement: Defines an entity-merge event requiring preserved history.

rows.anchor: Before confirmation x !=_known y. After confirmation x=y. Historical records may have been created under separate identities. We need to preserve HistoricalIdentityState
rows.statement: Requires preserving historical identity state across a merge confirmation.

rows.anchor: we previously believed x=y. New evidence shows x!=y. We need Split(x,t). This is extremely important
rows.statement: Defines an entity-split event as extremely important for correcting prior false merges.

rows.anchor: A false merge can contaminate downstream knowledge. After splitting, we may need ImpactAnalysis over every assertion depending on the merged identity. IdentityRevision -> KnowledgeRevision
rows.statement: States identity revision requires downstream knowledge-revision impact analysis given contamination risk.

rows.anchor: A -> Entity(x) and later x -> {x_1,x_2}, then A may need re-evaluation
rows.statement: Formalizes identity-revision propagation to dependent assertions after an entity split.

rows.anchor: Closure(Assumption). Now Closure(Identity). Thus AffectedKnowledge(x) can be computed
rows.statement: Extends the closure operation from assumptions to identity, enabling computation of affected knowledge.

rows.anchor: G_I=(E,R) where E are entities and R include relations such as sameAs, aliasOf, instanceOf, versionOf, deployedOn, replacedBy, relatedTo
rows.statement: Formally defines the identity graph with seven relation kinds.

rows.anchor: sameAs may be intended as identity/equivalence. But relatedTo is not. And versionOf is directional. Therefore relation semantics must be explicit
rows.statement: States not all identity-graph relations are equivalence relations; semantics must be explicit per relation.

rows.anchor: If a relation ~ satisfies x~x, x~y=>y~x, x~y and y~z=>x~z, then it is an equivalence relation. This allows equivalence classes
rows.statement: Formally defines the equivalence-relation criteria enabling equivalence classes.

rows.anchor: [x] represents the equivalence class of x. All aliases can then map to CanonicalEntity([x])
rows.statement: Defines identity equivalence classes and canonical-entity mapping.

rows.anchor: Not every same relation should be transitive. sameVersionFamily may not mean sameExactArtifact. Therefore each relation needs formal semantics
rows.statement: Warns against assuming transitivity for every 'same'-labeled relation, worked with a version-family example.

rows.anchor: Server has 31GB RAM and MemoryCapacity=31GB. These may be semantically equivalent. But semantic equivalence is not necessarily entity identity
rows.statement: Distinguishes semantic (statement) equivalence from entity identity.

rows.anchor: S_1 equiv S_2 if they express the same proposition under the same context. This is different from S_1=S_2
rows.statement: Formally defines statement equivalence as distinct from entity equality.

rows.anchor: Two propositions may be equivalent in Context_A but not Context_B. Therefore Equivalence(S_1,S_2,C)
rows.statement: Defines contextual equivalence between propositions.

rows.anchor: 1 GB versus 1024 MB. Depending on whether GB means decimal or binary units, 1GB != 1024MB under SI conventions. Therefore normalization must preserve semantic units
rows.statement: Worked unit-ambiguity example requiring semantics-preserving normalization.

rows.anchor: x=1m and x=100cm can be transformed into a common unit. Then equality can be established through Normalization(x)=Normalization(y)
rows.statement: Defines mathematical normalization as a route to establishing equality across units.

rows.anchor: 03/04/2026. Is this 3 April or March 4? Without locale/context, normalization is ambiguous. Thus Normalization is itself an epistemic operation
rows.statement: Worked date-format ambiguity example establishing normalization as itself an epistemic operation.

rows.anchor: Reference->Parsing->Normalization->Context Resolution->Candidate Generation->Evidence Comparison->Dependency Check->Identity Inference->Validation->Identity State->Canonicalization
rows.statement: Presents an eleven-stage identity-resolution pipeline.

rows.anchor: For N entities, naive pairwise comparison is O(N^2). Large knowledge bases make this expensive
rows.statement: Analyzes the computational cost of naive pairwise entity comparison.

rows.anchor: blocking: CandidatePairs subset E x E. Only plausible pairs are evaluated. sameDomain or sameSerialPrefix
rows.statement: Defines blocking to restrict entity-resolution candidate pairs.

rows.anchor: feasible on a normal PC if we use indexing; blocking; caching; incremental resolution; graph partitioning. The mathematical model itself does not require enormous infrastructure
rows.statement: Validates computational feasibility of the identity-resolution architecture on ordinary hardware given standard techniques.

rows.anchor: P(Match|X) can be estimated. But the model needs training data; assumptions; calibration; context. Otherwise a probability is merely decorative
rows.statement: Warns probabilistic matching without training data/calibration/context produces merely decorative probabilities.

rows.anchor: p >= tau_confirm => Confirmed. But tau_confirm must depend on the cost of false merging
rows.statement: Defines threshold-based identity confirmation dependent on false-merge cost.

rows.anchor: C_FM false-merge cost and C_FS false-split cost. Then the threshold should reflect C_FM,C_FS. This is much more principled than choosing tau=0.9 arbitrarily
rows.statement: Formalizes cost-sensitive threshold selection, correcting arbitrary fixed-threshold practice.

rows.anchor: choose among Confirm, Reject, Investigate, Abstain. based on expected loss. This is another direct application of Steps 34 and 35
rows.statement: Extends decision-theoretic expected-loss reasoning (Steps 34-35) into a four-option identity-resolution decision.

rows.anchor: P(Same)=0.85. We could InvestigateDNS at low cost. If DNS can resolve the ambiguity, the VOI may be high. Thus identity resolution becomes an active epistemic process
rows.statement: Worked DNS-investigation example framing identity resolution as an active, VOI-driven epistemic process.

rows.anchor: What evidence would most efficiently distinguish x=y from x!=y? This is exactly Step 34's NextBestEpistemicAction
rows.statement: Explicitly identifies identity resolution as an instance of the Next-Best-Epistemic-Action problem.

rows.anchor: Experiments 1-6: highly similar names in different bounded contexts->no automatic global merge PASS; different references provably identify same server->sameEntity link PASS; same hostname different environments->identity remains contextual/ambiguous PASS; IP address changes while server identity co
rows.statement: Runs falsification tests 1-6 (all PASS): similar-but-cross-context names are not automatically globally merged; provably-same-entity distinct references can be linked via sameAs; same-hostname-different-environment references remain contextually ambiguous; an IP change is correctly classified as state change rather than identity change; version relationships are correctly typed as versionOf rather than exact-artifact identity; and high-but-not-certain match probability remains candidate/probable pending policy-based confirmation.

experiment.hypothesis: The identity-resolution model correctly avoids premature/incorrect merges while correctly linking provably-same entities and distinguishing state from identity and version from exact-artifact identity.
experiment.setup: Six scenarios each isolating one property.
experiment.assumptions: n/a
experiment.inputs: n/a
experiment.method: apply the contextual-identity/state-vs-identity/versioning/confidence-threshold rules to each scenario
experiment.result: all six produce the theoretically expected outcome
experiment.interpretation: confirms these six core identity-resolution properties
experiment.limitations: illustrative, not executed
experiment.conclusion: All six tests PASS.

rows.anchor: Experiments 7-12: confirmed merge later falsified->split/identity revision plus downstream impact analysis PASS; evidence records from different references resolving to same entity->potentially aggregated subject to independence analysis PASS; similar statements using different units->normalization
rows.statement: Runs falsification tests 7-12 (all PASS): a falsified merge correctly triggers split plus downstream impact analysis; cross-reference same-entity evidence is combinable subject to independence analysis; unit-mismatched statements require normalization before equivalence; locale-ambiguous dates are not silently normalized; non-transitive similarity does not trigger automatic equivalence-class merging; and a false merge's downstream impact is fully identified via identity closure.

experiment.hypothesis: The model correctly handles merge falsification/impact analysis, evidence aggregation across resolved references, normalization gating, non-transitive similarity, and identity-closure impact tracing.
experiment.setup: Six scenarios each isolating one property.
experiment.assumptions: n/a
experiment.inputs: n/a
experiment.method: apply the split/aggregation/normalization/transitivity/closure rules to each scenario
experiment.result: all six produce the theoretically expected outcome
experiment.interpretation: confirms these six additional identity-resolution properties
experiment.limitations: illustrative, not executed
experiment.conclusion: All six tests PASS.

rows.anchor: STEP 38 — PASS. This is an important milestone because we have formalized something that is often hidden inside ordinary software systems: Identity is itself knowledge
rows.statement: Step 38 self-verdict: PASS, establishing identity as itself knowledge.

rows.anchor: Similarity != Identity ... Reference != Entity ... RealWorldIdentity != DomainIdentity ... Probabilistic identity must not silently become confirmed identity ... Identity is contextual ... Identity changes require temporal history ... Identity revision requires downstream impact analysis ... False m
rows.statement: States eight core boxed Step 38 principles covering similarity/identity, reference/entity, real-world/domain identity, probabilistic-vs-confirmed identity, contextuality, temporal history, impact analysis, false merge/split, and evidence-first canonicalization.

rows.anchor: REALITY->OBSERVATION->REFERENCE (Normalization/Context)->ENTITY RESOLUTION (Similarity/Evidence/Provenance)->IDENTITY INFERENCE (Confirmed/Unknown -> Canonical Identity/Investigation)->KNOWLEDGE (Claims/Models/Decisions)->VALIDATION->OUTCOME->META-VALIDATION
rows.statement: Presents an updated end-to-end architecture diagram incorporating reference/entity-resolution/identity-inference stages.

rows.anchor: Knowledge graph G_K ... Provenance/dependency graph G_P ... Identity graph G_I ... These graphs must interact but must not be collapsed into one undifferentiated graph
rows.statement: States the three-graph architectural distinction: knowledge, provenance/dependency, and identity graphs must interact without collapsing.

rows.anchor: KnowledgeOS = G_K + G_P + G_I + TemporalState + EpistemicControl rather than simply KnowledgeOS=KnowledgeGraph
rows.statement: Formalizes KnowledgeOS as a five-component architecture rather than a single knowledge graph.

lexical.anchor: If identity is wrong, then Evidence->Claim->Model->Decision can all be mathematically correct about the wrong object. That is one of the most dangerous classes of epistemic failure

formal.anchor: denotes:R->E. r_1=r_2 is not required for denotes(r_1)=denotes(r_2). Different references can identify the same entity

operational.anchor: Experiments 1-6: highly similar names in different bounded contexts->no automatic global merge PASS; different references provably identify same server->sameEntity link PASS; same hostname different environments->identity remains contextual/ambiguous PASS; IP address changes while server identity co

rationale_evidence.anchor: If identity is wrong, then Evidence->Claim->Model->Decision can all be mathematically correct about the wrong object. That is one of the most dangerous classes of epistemic failure
rationale_evidence.statement: Frames identity error as one of the most dangerous epistemic failure classes: correct reasoning about the wrong object.

rationale_evidence.anchor: We should therefore reject the idea that identity resolution is merely a database lookup ... when identity is ambiguous IdentityResolution is an epistemic inference problem
rationale_evidence.statement: Argues identity resolution is often an epistemic inference problem, not merely a database lookup.

rationale_evidence.anchor: For N entities, naive pairwise comparison is O(N^2). Large knowledge bases make this expensive
rationale_evidence.statement: Analyzes the computational cost of naive pairwise entity comparison.

sources.note: A general, non-Bayesian-specific formalization of the Zero Lens as an epistemic/architectural discipline (not a domain object) with a ten-item invariant catalog ZI-01..ZI-10, a formal definition, a DDD one-liner, and an operational recursive Zero cycle; distinguished from the indexed zero-lens-bayesian-gaps object, which is specifically the 12 gaps (ZERO-01..12) found by applying Zero to Bayesian cognitive modelling — this document instead states Zero as a general foundational lens for the whole KnowledgeOS model.

rows.anchor: Zero Lens examines the boundary between what a KnowledgeOS knowledge state represents and what it does not represent. ... What is absent, undefined, unobserved, undiscovered, unresolved, unmodelled, assumed away, or otherwise outside the current representation? ... Not represented ⇒ Does not exist ... That inference is generally invalid. ... a discipline of non-collapse.
rows.statement: States the Zero Lens's purpose: examine the boundary of what a knowledge state represents vs does not, explicitly to block the invalid inference 'not represented ⇒ does not exist'; names it a 'discipline of non-collapse' that protects distinctions ordinary information systems routinely destroy.
invariants: Not represented ⇒ Does not exist (this inference is generally invalid)

rows.anchor:
Zero 
eq KnowledgeElement ... Zero 
eq Dimension ... Zero 
eq Value ... Zero is a constraint on interpretation.
rows.statement: First architectural principle: Zero must not be modelled as a domain object/knowledge element/dimension/value sitting alongside Knowledge/Dimension/Statement/Value in a hierarchy; it is a lens applied to the knowledge state (Z(K_t)) and a constraint on interpretation, not a data field.

rows.anchor: Dependency(X)=Present / Absent / Unknown ... A conventional database often collapses B and C into: NULL. KnowledgeOS must not. ... these are different epistemic axes ... Zero is pushing us toward orthogonal semantic properties, rather than a single status field.
rows.statement: Argues a dimension's epistemic state needs several orthogonal axes (Dimension, Assessment, Value, Evidence), not one enum collapsing 'investigated-and-absent' and 'never-established' into a single NULL — giving worked contrasting examples of the same dimension under different Assessment/Value/Evidence combinations.

rows.anchor:
NO_EVIDENCE 
eq INVALID_EVIDENCE ... NOT_ASSESSED 
eq LOW_CONFIDENCE ... coverage gap ... epistemic uncertainty ... NOT_APPLICABLE 
eq UNKNOWN
rows.statement: Establishes three further non-collapse distinctions with worked examples: no-evidence vs invalid/unreliable evidence; not-assessed (a coverage gap) vs low-confidence (an epistemic uncertainty after assessment); and not-applicable (evaluated and outside domain) vs unknown.

rows.anchor: Zero tells us not to resolve the contradiction merely by selecting one value. ... Claims(Version)={c_1,c_2} with Conflict(c_1,c_2)=True ... KnowledgeOS should present both information and warn the owner rather than silently deciding which information is correct. ... Conflict \neq Unknown ... Conflict \neq Invalid
rows.statement: When two trusted sources conflict (e.g. Version=2.69 vs 3.85), Zero requires preserving the conflict as a first-class claim set with an explicit Conflict flag rather than silently picking a winner; a conflict is itself information about the current epistemic state, distinct from both Unknown and Invalid.

rows.anchor: The derived statement is not directly observed. It is logically produced. ... Observed -> Evidence ... Derived -> Rule + premises ... The fact that a derived value is absent does not mean the underlying condition is absent.
rows.statement: Using a worked compliance-rule example (Version=2.69, RequiredVersion=3.85, Rule ⇒ Compliance=False), shows Zero must preserve the distinction between an observed statement (backed by Evidence) and a derived statement (backed by Rule+premises); absence of a derived value does not mean the underlying condition is absent.

rows.anchor: What semantic relationships might this sentence fail to express? ... Not expressed \neq False ... Semantically unresolved \neq Semantically absent ... one of the strongest intersections between the Sanskrit lens and Zero.
rows.statement: Applies Zero to semantic/Pāṇinian parsing: a parsed sentence (e.g. 'Nexus runs version 2.69 on RHEL 9.8') expresses only certain relationships; the parser must not manufacture unexpressed implications (e.g. a specific kernel version); states Not expressed ≠ False and Semantically unresolved ≠ Semantically absent, called one of the strongest intersections between the Sanskrit/semantic lens and Zero.

rows.anchor: "secure" may conceal many dimensions ... Which dimensions have been compressed into the word "secure"? ... Abstraction \neq Completeness ... Compression \neq Losslessness ... documents, embeddings, summaries and AI responses are all forms of compression.
rows.statement: A high-level word like 'secure' can legitimately compress many sub-dimensions (authentication, authorization, network exposure, vulnerabilities, encryption, dependencies, patch status, configuration) without falsifying them; states the general rules Abstraction ≠ Completeness and Compression ≠ Losslessness, explicitly warning that documents, embeddings, summaries and AI responses are all forms of compression subject to this rule.

rows.anchor: I found no evidence of an undocumented dependency. ... NoEvidence \Rightarrow NoDependency ... Zero rejects that inference. ... AI must be evaluated not only on: What did it extract? but also: What did it fail to discover?
rows.statement: Applies Zero to AI evaluation specifically: an AI's 'no evidence found' must not be interpreted as 'no dependency exists'; argues AI systems must be evaluated on what they failed to discover, not only on what they extracted, calling this a fundamentally different evaluation problem.

rows.anchor: Dimension discovery / Value determination / Relationship discovery / Derivation / Contradiction detection / Assumption detection / Coverage analysis / Lens variation ... TryBest = Maximize justified knowledge expansion while preserving unresolved boundaries
rows.statement: Operationalizes the instruction 'try your best' into eight concrete sub-disciplines (dimension discovery, value determination, relationship discovery, derivation, contradiction detection, assumption detection, coverage analysis, lens variation), summarized as TryBest = Maximize justified knowledge expansion while preserving unresolved boundaries — explicitly contrasted with just telling an LLM to 'be comprehensive'.

rows.anchor: Every lens must be accompanied by an explicit examination of its blind spots. ... Normal lens: L_i(O) -> D_i ... Zero: Z(L_i,O) -> Boundary(L_i) ... Are there dimensions outside security that affect the security determination?
rows.statement: Formalizes Zero as a meta-lens applied to every other lens: a normal lens L_i(O) -> D_i must be paired with Z(L_i,O) -> Boundary(L_i), i.e. every lens must be examined for what it systematically fails to see, what assumptions it makes, and what dimensions lie outside its scope — guarding against e.g. '100 security dimensions found' being mistaken for 'security is comprehensively understood'.

type_signature.domain: a lens L_i applied to observation O

rows.anchor: Known gap: d \in D^*\setminus D_t ... Unknown gap: D^*\setminus D_t is itself partially unknown. That is the deepest form of Zero. ... Zero(K_t) may itself contain unresolved structure.
rows.statement: Distinguishes a 'known gap' (a specific missing dimension d ∈ D*\D_t is identified) from an 'unknown gap' (D*\D_t is itself partially unknown, i.e. we don't know which dimensions are missing), and generalizes this to recursive uncertainty about unknown dimensions, unknown relationships, and unknown interpretations — concluding Zero(K_t) may itself contain unresolved structure and therefore should not be an ordinary database field.

rows.anchor:
Mithya 
eq Asat ... Appearing/not independently concrete ≠ nonexistent. ... Representation 
eq Reality ... Model insufficiency 
eq Reality insufficiency ... a powerful Zero safeguard against reification.
rows.statement: Translates the philosophical Mithya≠Asat distinction into a Zero safeguard against reification: Representation ≠ Reality, Model insufficiency ≠ Reality insufficiency — a missing dimension in the model does not mean the corresponding aspect of the observed object does not exist, nor does difficulty establishing a statement mean the underlying phenomenon is unreal.

rows.anchor: Claim=(Dimension,Value,Context,Time) at minimum. ... NotCurrentlyTrue \Rightarrow WasNeverTrue ... PreviouslyUnknown \Rightarrow PreviouslyNonexistent ... essential for knowledge history.
rows.statement: Extends Zero to temporal knowledge: a Claim must minimally carry (Dimension, Value, Context, Time); Zero must block both 'not currently true ⇒ was never true' and 'previously unknown ⇒ previously nonexistent', framed as essential for knowledge history.

rows.anchor: I would not create a `Zero` aggregate. Instead, Zero should influence the ubiquitous language and invariants around knowledge. ... An unassessed dimension must not be interpreted as absent. ... A representation must not be treated as the observed reality.
rows.statement: From a DDD standpoint, explicitly rules out a 'Zero' aggregate/entity; instead Zero should shape the ubiquitous language and invariants across Observation/Dimension/Statement/Claim/Value/Evidence/Source/Assessment/Derivation/Conflict/Uncertainty/Coverage/Assumption/Context/Validity/TemporalValidity, listing five example invariants (unassessed≠absent, absence-of-evidence≠evidence-of-absence, unresolved≠false, derived statements retain derivation basis, representation≠observed reality).

rows.anchor: ZI-01 — Non-collapse of absence: Unknown ≠ Absent ... ZI-06 — Non-collapse of dimension/value: UnknownDimension ≠ UnknownValue ... ZI-10 — Non-collapse of completeness: NoKnownGap ≠ Complete
rows.statement: Presents a formal ten-item invariant catalog ZI-01..ZI-10 (Non-collapse of: absence Unknown≠Absent; assessment NotAssessed≠LowConfidence; applicability NotApplicable≠Unknown; evidence NoEvidence≠InvalidEvidence; interpretation Unresolved≠False; dimension/value UnknownDimension≠UnknownValue; representation/reality Model≠Reality; state/time PreviouslyUnknown≠PreviouslyAbsent; conflict Conflict≠Invalidity; completeness NoKnownGap≠Complete), flagging ZI-10 as especially important.

rows.anchor: |D_t|/|D^*| is not a useful completeness measure. ... Coverage(K,U) = |D_{assessed}|/|D_U| ... provided D_U is explicitly defined. ... Completeness requires a defined universe of discourse.
rows.statement: Rejects |D_t|/|D*| as a completeness measure when |D*|=∞ (e.g. 'KnowledgeOS knows 95%' is meaningless globally), and instead proposes a bounded-domain Coverage(K,U) = |D_assessed|/|D_U| valid only when D_U (the universe of discourse) is explicitly defined; states 'completeness requires a defined universe of discourse' as a mathematically important restriction.

type_signature.domain: knowledge state K, bounded domain U

invariants: Completeness requires a defined universe of discourse

rows.anchor: Zero is not: "We don't know anything." Nor: "Knowledge is impossible." It is: "Do not claim more than the represented epistemic state justifies." ... Zero actually enables more aggressive knowledge discovery.
rows.statement: Explicitly distinguishes Zero from epistemic pessimism: Zero does not claim knowledge is impossible or that nothing is known; it only forbids claiming more than the represented state justifies — and argues this actually enables MORE aggressive knowledge discovery, since the system can safely mark a dimension unknown and keep searching rather than prematurely declaring non-existence.

rows.anchor: CURRENT KNOWLEDGE -> ZERO EXAMINATION -> Missing values/Missing dimensions/Hidden assumptions -> More evidence/New lenses/Model challenge -> RE-EVALUATE -> NEW KNOWLEDGE -> Zero again ... Zero is recursive. It does not run once during ingestion.
rows.statement: Defines an operational, recursive 'Zero cycle': current knowledge -> Zero examination (missing values / missing dimensions / hidden assumptions) -> remediation (more evidence / new lenses / model challenge) -> re-evaluate -> new knowledge -> Zero again; explicitly states Zero is continuously applicable, not a one-time ingestion-time check.

rows.anchor: The Zero Lens is an epistemic and architectural discipline that examines the boundary of a knowledge state ... while explicitly preventing those conditions from being interpreted as non-existence, falsity, invalidity, irrelevance or completeness. ... Zero is the lens that prevents the domain model from turning epistemic absence into a domain fact. ... ZERO PRINCIPLE: What is not represented is not thereby nonexistent.
rows.statement: Gives the document's final formal definition of the Zero Lens, a one-line DDD formulation ('Zero is the lens that prevents the domain model from turning epistemic absence into a domain fact'), and a capstone 'ZERO PRINCIPLE' ('What is not represented is not thereby nonexistent') with a restated set of seven boxed non-collapse rules, concluding Zero is 'not a model of nothingness, but a rigorous discipline for preserving the boundary between what the system knows, what it has not established, and what it has not even yet learned to ask.'
invariants: What is not represented is not thereby nonexistent.

rows.anchor: Lord is a philosophical lens for observing Knowledge Space as potentially infinite and non-exhaustible. ... Zero asks: What is missing from this knowledge state? ... Lord asks: What is the nature of the space toward which this knowledge state is trying to become more complete?
rows.statement: Defines the Lord Lens rigorously and distinguishes its purpose from Zero's: Lord observes the knowledge space as an ideal, unbounded whole against which every finite knowledge state is partial (asking about the nature of the target space), while Zero asks what is missing from the current state (a boundary/gap question) — explicitly not a claim that KnowledgeOS models God or consciousness.

rows.anchor:
Ontology: What exists in the observed reality? R ... Epistemology: What do we know about it? K(R) ... d
otin K_t with d
otin R ... Absence from Knowledge 
eq Absence from Reality
rows.statement: Formalizes the ontology/epistemology separation as the Lord Lens's strongest philosophical contribution: reality R vs knowledge-about-it K(R); explicitly warns not to confuse d∉K_t (absent from current knowledge) with d∉R (absent from reality) — Absence from Knowledge ≠ Absence from Reality, connecting Lord Lens directly to Zero Lens.
invariants: Absence from Knowledge ≠ Absence from Reality

rows.anchor: Lord: Ω, the ideal knowledge/reality space. Zero: Ω-K_t ... Lord defines the horizon. Zero examines our inability to see the entire horizon.
rows.statement: Describes Lord and Zero as near mathematically dual: Lord = Ω (the ideal space), Zero = Ω−K_t (the boundary, itself partially unknown since Ω is not fully enumerable); Lord defines the horizon, Zero examines the system's inability to see the entire horizon.

rows.anchor: Lord is the horizon of knowledge, not a record inside the knowledge base. ... \Omega \neq \bigcup_{t}K_t even if we continue learning forever. ... Lord -> Completeness Seeking ... Zero -> Completeness Humility ... Seek the whole without ever claiming that the current representation is the whole.
rows.statement: Restates the refined definition (Lord is the horizon of knowledge, not a record inside the knowledge base, and Ω ≠ ∪_t K_t even under unbounded learning) and closes by naming Lord and Zero the two foundational meta-lenses: Lord drives completeness-seeking (prevents premature closure), Zero drives completeness-humility (prevents false certainty); together: seek the whole without ever claiming the current representation is the whole.
invariants: Ω ≠ ∪_t K_t even under unbounded learning

rows.anchor: There are about 28 different hellish planets in total ... The text represents the existence of these systems but does not represent their details — they are underdescribed. ... What is represented only at the level of existence, not at the level of detail?
rows.statement: Adds a new Zero facet: a dimension/entity can be represented only at the level of its existence (it is asserted to be there) while remaining entirely underdescribed at the level of detail — a representation gap distinct from unknown-value or unknown-dimension.

rows.anchor: Vishnuloka is 400,000 miles in circumference, and inaccessible for any mortal living being. ... Some knowledge is inaccessible by current means — but that does not mean it doesn't exist. ... Inaccessible \neq Non-existent
rows.statement: Adds a new Zero non-collapse pair not previously catalogued in ZI-01..10: Inaccessible ≠ Non-existent — a dimension/realm can be currently unreachable by available means without that implying it does not exist.

rows.anchor:
Inaccessible 
eq Nonexistent ... I would generalize it: Not Observed 
eq Not Existing ... Not Known 
eq Not Existing ... Not Represented 
eq Not Existing ... Not Accessible 
eq Not Existing ... Not Assessed 
eq Not Applicable
rows.statement: Generalizes S0727's 'Inaccessible ≠ Nonexistent' into a family of five non-collapse rules: Not Observed ≠ Not Existing; Not Known ≠ Not Existing; Not Represented ≠ Not Existing; Not Accessible ≠ Not Existing; Not Assessed ≠ Not Applicable — framed as where Zero becomes an epistemic safety mechanism.

rows.anchor: Could the classification itself be incomplete? ... Zero does not merely inspect Values. It can inspect: The model of dimensions itself.
rows.statement: Argues Zero must be able to inspect the dimension-classification model itself (e.g. 'are three represented states the complete set, or could there be a fourth?'), not only the values assigned to already-recognized dimensions.

rows.anchor: the knowledge state needs not just Time but potentially TemporalContext and ObservationTime, AssessmentTime, DecisionTime, ValidityPeriod.
rows.statement: Extends the temporal knowledge model from a single Time field to five distinct temporal fields: TemporalContext, ObservationTime, AssessmentTime, DecisionTime, ValidityPeriod — a significant architectural consequence of cross-level temporal non-uniformity.

rows.anchor: LORD = space expansion ... ZERO = boundary awareness ... KnowledgeOS must continuously expand its model toward the ideal knowledge space while continuously exposing the fact that its current model is only a partial representation.
rows.statement: Restates the precise division of labor between the two lenses with expanded activity lists — Lord drives dimensional discovery, model expansion, multiple lenses, hierarchical modelling, contextual modelling, recursive discovery, pursuit of completeness; Zero detects unknown dimensions/values/relationships, inaccessible information, unresolved reasoning, hidden assumptions, model boundaries, false completeness — summarized as Lord=space expansion, Zero=boundary awareness.

rows.anchor: Q1: What is an "observation"? ... Q3: What is a "dimension"? ... Primitive Dimension / Derived Dimension / Relationship Dimension / Meta Dimension ... Q12: What are the semantics of 0, 1, and ? (Unknown)? ... Q17: Can dimensions contain dimensions? ... How deep can this go? Is there a bottom? ... Q24: When does knowledge become sufficient for a decision?
rows.statement: Catalogs 24 explicitly numbered open questions across 8 categories (A.Ontology Q1-5: observation/state/dimension/value/relationship, including a proposed four-way dimension typology of Primitive/Derived/Relationship/Meta; B.Epistemology Q6-11: knowledge/fact/evidence/reason/determination/uncertainty; C.Logic Q12-14: semantics of 0/1/undetermined, contradiction representation, permissible inference forms; D.Infinite-Space Q15-18: what Ω/D* precisely are, hierarchical-dimension recursion depth, discovery mechanisms; E.Zero Q19-20: formal Zero output schema and semantics of each absence-type; F.Lord Q21: the boundary between philosophical lens and mathematical architecture; G.Evolution Q22-23: what exactly gets recalculated on a new dimension, state-change vs knowledge-change; H.Decision Q24: when knowledge becomes sufficient for a decision, independent of completeness), each marked Undefined/Partially defined, with an 8-phase priority research order (Ontology -> Epistemology -> Logic -> Infinite Space -> Zero -> Lord -> Evolution -> Decision).

rows.anchor: Actual completeness D_t=D^* ... Demonstrated completeness: We have evidence that the relevant bounded universe has been exhausted. ... Apparent completeness: No further dimensions have currently been discovered. ... Zero should prevent ApparentComplete \Rightarrow Complete
rows.statement: Introduces a three-way completeness taxonomy: Actual completeness (D_t=D*, generally unknowable), Demonstrated completeness (evidence that a defined bounded universe has been exhausted), and Apparent completeness (no further dimensions currently discovered, the weakest and most dangerous kind) — explicitly requiring Zero to block the inference ApparentComplete ⇒ Complete.

rows.anchor: Contradiction = a boundary in the field, not in Ω ... Contradictions: Exist within the field (K_t); Are resolved from Ω (the Knower's perspective); Should be preserved, not prematurely resolved.
rows.statement: Restates the earlier Zero-lens contradiction-preservation principle in Gita vocabulary: contradictions exist within the finite field K_t, not in Ω itself, and should be preserved as boundary conditions rather than prematurely resolved.

rows.anchor: Evidence from Trust(E) from Quality(E) from Relevance(E,P) ... KnowledgeOS should not simply select the trusted source. It should preserve both and reason about the conflict. ... ZeroReason=CONFLICTING_EVIDENCE
rows.statement: Refines the evidence model into four separable properties (raw Evidence, Trust(E), Quality(E), Relevance(E,P)); formalizes conflicting evidence as a first-class epistemic condition (E1⇒P, E2⇒¬P yields Determination(P)=? tagged ZeroReason=CONFLICTING_EVIDENCE) rather than arbitrarily picking the more-trusted source, aligning with the earlier 'present both, warn the owner' principle.

rows.anchor: Zero-1 — Value boundary: d known, v=? ... Zero-2 — Dimension boundary: d\notin D_t ... Zero-3 — Relationship boundary: R(d_1,d_2)=? ... Zero-4 — Representation boundary: the underlying phenomenon cannot currently be represented adequately by our model. R\not\rightarrow K_t ... This fourth category is particularly important.
rows.statement: Formalizes four distinct Zero boundaries: Zero-1 value boundary (dimension known, value unknown), Zero-2 dimension boundary (dimension not in D_t), Zero-3 relationship boundary (dimensions known, relationship unknown), and Zero-4 representation boundary (R ↛ K_t — the underlying phenomenon cannot currently be adequately represented by the model at all, distinct from the other three and flagged as particularly important).

rows.anchor: We currently represent 127 recognized dimensions of Nexus. Of these, 109 have direct system evidence, 12 are supported by trusted external sources, and 6 remain unresolved. ... That is far more meaningful than: "We have 85% knowledge."
rows.statement: Gives a worked business-communication example: instead of answering 'how much do we know about Nexus?' with a single percentage, KnowledgeOS should answer with a structured breakdown (recognized dimension count, evidence-support breakdown, unresolved count, relationship coverage, count of areas where the dimensional model itself may be incomplete, and an explicit statement of decision-sufficiency vs completeness) — illustrating the practical payoff of the whole Lord+Zero+decision-sufficiency model.

rows.anchor: The Gita does not prove our Infinite Knowledge Space theory. ... Lord Lens: There is always a larger space against which the current model must be understood. ... Zero Lens: Never confuse the boundary of our representation with the boundary of reality. That last sentence is, in my view, one of the strongest formulations we have reached so far.
rows.statement: Closes with eight boxed design hypotheses (reality≠representation; observed field richer than a flat fact list; observer/knower must be distinguished from observed; knowledge≠mere facts; completeness≠decision-sufficiency; trust/evidence/truth/confidence/knowledge-quality must not be collapsed; new dimensions can invalidate model adequacy without falsifying prior observations) and names the capstone formulation 'never confuse the boundary of our representation with the boundary of reality' as one of the strongest reached so far, explicitly noting the Gita does not prove the Infinite Knowledge Space theory but supplies coherent design hypotheses.
invariants: Never confuse the boundary of our representation with the boundary of reality.

rows.anchor: Contradiction(P)=? needs context, time, proposition identity, and perhaps observer identity. ... P(C_1)=1 and P(C_2)=0 be a contradiction? Probably not.
rows.statement: Argues 'contradiction' itself has never been formally defined: same-context-same-time P=1 and P=0 is a genuine contradiction, but differing-context P(C1)=1 / P(C2)=0 probably is not; Contradiction(P) needs to be parameterized by context, time, proposition identity, and possibly observer identity.

rows.anchor: Zero should probably explicitly distinguish: UNKNOWN, ABSENT, FALSE, NOT_ASSESSED, NOT_APPLICABLE, UNDEFINED, CONFLICTING, INACCESSIBLE, UNREPRESENTABLE. These are still not formally defined.
rows.statement: Lists nine Zero output states (UNKNOWN, ABSENT, FALSE, NOT_ASSESSED, NOT_APPLICABLE, UNDEFINED, CONFLICTING, INACCESSIBLE, UNREPRESENTABLE) as still lacking formal definitions, despite the many non-collapse pairs already established between subsets of them.

rows.anchor: Can we upgrade Nexus? ... KnowledgeOS should not simply answer: YES or NO. It should expose: WHAT WE KNOW / WHAT WE DO NOT KNOW / WHAT WE MAY NOT HAVE CONSIDERED / WHAT WE THINK / WHY / WHAT COULD CHANGE THE DETERMINATION / DECISION: Human / authorized owner.
rows.statement: Gives a concrete worked structured-answer template for a decision question ('Can we upgrade Nexus?') that a system must never answer with a bare YES/NO: it must expose what is known, what is not known, what may not even have been considered, the current provisional view and its reasoning, what could change the determination, and that the decision itself belongs to the human/authorized owner.

rows.anchor: Known context + Unknown state -> Inquiry ... The current knowledge state has an unresolved dimension.
rows.statement: Derives from Dhṛtarāṣṭra's opening question a first Zero pattern: Known context + Unknown state -> Inquiry, i.e. the correct Zero-lens reading of 'what happened?' is 'the current knowledge state has an unresolved dimension', not 'nothing is known' or 'the answer is false'.

rows.anchor: When new knowledge invalidates the Knower's current determination, the system should expose the conflict rather than silently resolve it. ... Previous determination -> New dimension discovered -> Existing determination affected -> Conflict/uncertainty -> Present both states -> Human Knower decides
rows.statement: States the principle that when new knowledge invalidates the Knower's current determination, the system must expose the conflict rather than silently resolve it, formalized as a six-step pipeline ending in 'Human Knower decides', consistent with the earlier 'present both, warn the owner' rule.

rows.anchor: Reality(d)=v while Knowledge_{Dhṛtarāṣṭra}(d)=? ... Unknown_{Knower}(d) rather than Unknown_{Reality}(d) ... KnowledgeOS does not create the state, and it does not become the Knower. It reduces the gap between what exists in the observed state and what the human Knower can understand about that state.
rows.statement: States the capstone formalization: a dimension can have a perfectly definite value in reality (Reality(d)=v) while the Knower's knowledge of it remains unresolved (Knowledge_Knower(d)=?) — Zero must represent Unknown_Knower(d) as distinct from Unknown_Reality(d); concludes 'KnowledgeOS does not create the state, and it does not become the Knower. It reduces the gap between what exists in the observed state and what the human Knower can understand about that state.'

type_signature.codomain: reality value vs Knower's knowledge state

rows.anchor: Zero in Sañjaya Layer asks: What do we not know about the state? ... Zero in Arjuna Layer asks: What does the Knower not know that prevents a sound understanding or decision? ... Zero_S = State Knowledge Gaps ... Zero_A = Understanding/Decision Gaps
rows.statement: Splits the Zero Lens into two layer-specific instances: Zero_S (State Knowledge Gaps — unknown dimension/value/relationship, missing evidence, source conflict, inaccessible system) operating in the Sañjaya layer, and Zero_A (Understanding/Decision Gaps — undefined ideal criterion, unknown business consequence, unresolved risk, unknown decision impact, unvalidated assumption, a new dimension that may change the determination) operating in the Arjuna layer.

rows.anchor: Sañjaya_K = (Observed, Inferred, Reported, Unknown, Conflicting, Unresolved) ... The system's raw output is not "truth"; it's a multi-faceted representation of epistemic status, preserving all its edges and ambiguities.
rows.statement: Formalizes the Sañjaya layer's output as a six-field epistemic-status tuple Sañjaya_K = (Observed, Inferred, Reported, Unknown, Conflicting, Unresolved), explicitly not a single truth value but a structure preserving every epistemic edge case.

rows.anchor: Zero (Z): Epistemic Hygiene ... It operates on both the Sañjaya Layer (Z_S ...) and the Arjuna Layer (Z_A ...). It also asks Z_Ideal - "What hasn't been specified in our ideal state?"
rows.statement: Adds a third Zero instance Z_Ideal ('what hasn't been specified in our ideal state?') alongside the already-established Z_S (Sañjaya-layer gaps) and Z_A (Arjuna-layer gaps), so Zero now operates on all three of state knowledge, understanding, and the ideal-state model itself.

rows.anchor: While speaking learned words, you are mourning for what is not worthy of grief. ... This is not a missing fact; it is a faulty model. ... The Arjuna Layer must be able to distinguish between "I don't know" (a missing dimension) and "I have misunderstood what I am observing" (a category error).
rows.statement: Reports Test 2 (I-don't-know vs I-have-misunderstood) as validated by Krishna's opening diagnosis (Gita 2.11): Arjuna's problem is not a missing fact but a category error (applying a grief-framework to an eternal soul); the Arjuna Layer/Krishna Lens must be able to diagnose and correct category errors, not merely fill in missing values.

rows.anchor: the Zero Lens and the Krishna Lens are not independent. They are two sides of the same epistemic coin. ... The Zero Lens creates the crisis, the "epistemic gap." ... The Krishna Lens then steps in to fill that gap. ... They are a dynamic duo in the epistemic lifecycle.
rows.statement: States a major new architectural insight from Chapter 2: the Zero Lens and Krishna Lens are interdependent, not independent — Zero's role is to create/identify the crisis or 'stuckness' (Arjuna's despair is Zero manifesting as a missing framework), and Krishna's role is to fill that identified gap with guiding knowledge that resolves the crisis; they function as a coupled pair in the epistemic lifecycle.

rows.anchor: What does "missing knowledge" mean when the missing thing is not merely a fact, but an entire dimension or conceptual framework that the Knower does not yet know exists? ... That is exactly where your earlier UNKNOWN \neq ABSENT distinction becomes extremely powerful.
rows.statement: Poses the next research question for the Zero Lens applied to Chapter 2: what does 'missing knowledge' mean when the missing thing is not a fact but an entire dimension or conceptual framework the Knower does not know exists — explicitly connecting this to the earlier UNKNOWN ≠ ABSENT distinction.

rows.anchor: Krishna Lens (K): Now split into two layers: 1. Entity Level (Ω): The source. 2. Role Level (Sārathi): The operational guidance mechanism. ... Z operates on both the Entity (Ω) and the Role (Sārathi) levels. It might ask, "What is missing from our understanding of the source?" or "Is the Sārathi role being performed correctly?"
rows.statement: Formalizes the Krishna Lens as split into an Entity Level (Ω, the source) and a Role Level (Sārathi, the operational guidance mechanism), and extends Zero to operate on BOTH levels — Zero can ask not only what is missing from understanding of the source, but also 'is the Sārathi role being performed correctly?', a role-adequacy question distinct from any prior Zero facet.

rows.anchor: It observes ... It exposes the current knowledge state ... It exposes Zero: What don't we know? And importantly: What don't we even know that we don't know? ... It applies the Lord Lens ... It guides inquiry ... It helps reinterpret ... It compares with the Knower's current ideal ... It progressively reduces relevant uncertainty: not U \rightarrow 0 but U_t \rightarrow U_{t+1}
rows.statement: Consolidates the Sārathi's functions into a ten-step list (observe [Sañjaya capability]; expose current knowledge state with evidence; expose Zero including unknown-unknowns; apply Lord Lens for undiscovered dimensions; guide inquiry toward the most worthwhile next investigation; help reinterpret existing dimensions when new ones appear; compare S_t against I_t; explain implications of the difference; progressively reduce relevant uncertainty U_t->U_{t+1}, never claiming U->0; help the Knower become ready to act), with KnowledgeOS ≠ DecisionOwner throughout.

rows.anchor: "Exposes Unknown Unknowns" ... If something is genuinely an unknown unknown, KnowledgeOS cannot directly expose it as a known missing thing. It can only expose: evidence that our current representation may be incomplete. ... Unknown dimension: D_known, V=? ... Suspected missing dimension: D=? ... Genuine unknown unknown: ?
rows.statement: Corrects S0748's 'exposes unknown unknowns' as internally inconsistent (a genuine unknown unknown cannot be directly exposed as a known missing thing — only evidence of possible incompleteness can be shown); introduces a refined three-way taxonomy: Unknown dimension (dimension known, value unknown), Suspected missing dimension (reason to believe the model may be incomplete, but no specific dimension named), and Genuine unknown unknown (no current awareness the dimension exists at all) — the Lord Lens is specifically for the third case.

lineage_claims.target: S0748's 'It exposes Zero: ... What don't we even know that we don't know?'
lineage_claims.quote: We should be careful here.

rows.anchor: Zero \rightarrow What is missing? ... Krishna \rightarrow What should we understand next? ... Current Knowledge -> ZERO -> What is missing? -> KRISHNA -> What knowledge should come next? -> Improved Understanding
rows.statement: Establishes an explicit sequencing: the Krishna Lens operates AFTER Zero — Zero identifies what is missing (dependency unknown, business impact unresolved, certificate relationship unclear) but does not itself decide what to do about it; Krishna then decides which of those uncertainties to investigate first and why.

rows.anchor: Guidance must inherit epistemic provenance ... Evidence, Inference, Hypothesis, Interpretation, Assumption, Recommendation ... If the underlying fact is uncertain, the guidance must not present the resulting conclusion as certain fact.
rows.statement: States that Krishna-Lens-produced guidance must inherit the epistemic provenance chain of its inputs (Evidence/Inference/Hypothesis/Interpretation/Assumption/Recommendation) — an uncertain underlying fact must never be presented in the resulting guidance as certain, directly following from the Zero-lens discipline.

rows.anchor: Zero: Detects absence / Identifies uncertainty / Exposes unresolved questions / Says "we don't know this" / Boundary detector ... Krishna: Responds to absence / Guides through uncertainty / Helps prioritize the next inquiry / Says "this is what we should understand next" / Navigation mechanism ... Zero = Epistemic Diagnosis ... Krishna = Epistemic Navigation
rows.statement: Gives a clean five-row Zero-vs-Krishna comparison table (detects vs responds to absence; identifies vs guides through uncertainty; exposes unresolved questions vs prioritizes next inquiry; 'we don't know this' vs 'this is what we should understand next'; boundary detector vs navigation mechanism), summarized as Zero=Epistemic Diagnosis, Krishna=Epistemic Navigation.

rows.anchor: KL(K_t,U_t,Z_t,I_t,P_t,C_t) \rightarrow (K_{t+1},U_{t+1},G_{t+1}) ... G_{t+1} \not\equiv Decision_{human} ... Lord: What else might exist? Zero: What is missing or unresolved? Krishna: What knowledge should guide us next? ... Sañjaya = What is the observed state? Sārathi = Guide the Knower through the knowledge journey. Arjuna = Understand, decide and act.
rows.statement: States the final formal Krishna Lens definition ('a lens for observing how knowledge becomes guidance for a Knower...while preserving uncertainty, provenance and human decision authority'), its six-argument function signature KL(K_t,U_t,Z_t,I_t,P_t,C_t)->(K_{t+1},U_{t+1},G_{t+1}), the critical invariant G_{t+1} ≢ Decision_human, and closes with what is called the cleanest formulation reached: Lord/Zero/Krishna as three questions and Sañjaya/Sārathi/Arjuna as three roles.

rows.statement: Formalizes the Knower/reality distinction: K_t (knowledge) ≠ X_t (reality) and K_t ≠ D; knowledge decomposes as K_t=(D^K_t, V^K_t), the represented dimension set and what's known of their values; a dimension absent from D^K_t does not imply it is absent from D — the mathematical form of UNKNOWN ≠ ABSENT.

rows.anchor: Known dimension, known value (d,v) ... Known dimension, unknown value (d,?) ... Known dimension, conflicting values (d,{v_1,v_2,...}) ... Suspected dimension (d,hypothesized) ... Dimension not represented d\notin D^K_t ... Explicitly assessed absent (d,ABSENT)
rows.statement: Formalizes six mathematically distinct dimension-value epistemic states: known dimension+known value (d,v); known dimension+unknown value (d,?); known dimension+conflicting values (d,{v1,v2,...}); suspected/hypothesized dimension; dimension not represented at all (d∉D^K_t); and explicitly assessed absent (d,ABSENT) — six states a single nullable field cannot represent.

rows.anchor: Z(K_t)=\{\text{known unknowns, unresolved assertions, conflicts, missing representations, assumptions}\} ... Z(K_t)=(U_t,C_t,A_t,M_t) ... Zero cannot simply calculate D-D^K_t because D itself is not completely known. Instead Zero operates on the boundary of the current model.
rows.statement: Gives Zero a rigorous mathematical definition: since D\D^K_t cannot actually be computed (D is not fully known), Zero instead operates on the boundary of the current model, formalized as Z(K_t)=(U_t,C_t,A_t,M_t) — unknown values, conflicts, unvalidated assumptions, and suspected-missing dimensions.

rows.anchor: Unknown -> Assumed -> Inferred -> Confirmed ... Unknown -> Conflicting -> Unresolved -> Rejected ... Suspected -> Unknown -> Inferred -> Confirmed
rows.statement: Proposes three illustrative epistemic-status transition paths for the eight-state epistemic-status algebra (Unknown->Assumed->Inferred->Confirmed; Unknown->Conflicting->Unresolved->Rejected; Suspected->Unknown->Inferred->Confirmed), offered as concrete examples rather than a complete formal transition system (still listed as an open 'algebra' to formalize).

rows.anchor: Version = unknown, Version = conflicting, Version = estimated, Version = range, Version = probability distribution, Version = not applicable ... Is each of these a value? Or is some of this epistemic status surrounding the value? This is a critical question.

What is absent, undefined, unobserved, undiscovered, unresolved, unmodelled, assumed away, or otherwise outside the current representation? ... Not represented ⇒ Does not exist ... That inference is generally invalid. ... a discipline of non-collapse.

governance.anchor: I would not create a `Zero` aggregate. Instead, Zero should influence the ubiquitous language and invariants around knowledge. ... An unassessed dimension must not be interpreted as absent. ... A representation must not be treated as the observed reality.

rationale_evidence.anchor: Dependency(X)=Present / Absent / Unknown ... A conventional database often collapses B and C into: NULL. KnowledgeOS must not. ... these are different epistemic axes ... Zero is pushing us toward orthogonal semantic properties, rather than a single status field.
rationale_evidence.statement: Argues a dimension's epistemic state needs several orthogonal axes (Dimension, Assessment, Value, Evidence), not one enum collapsing 'investigated-and-absent' and 'never-established' into a single NULL — giving worked contrasting examples of the same dimension under different Assessment/Value/Evidence combinations.

rationale_evidence.anchor: I found no evidence of an undocumented dependency. ... NoEvidence \Rightarrow NoDependency ... Zero rejects that inference. ... AI must be evaluated not only on: What did it extract? but also: What did it fail to discover?
rationale_evidence.statement: Applies Zero to AI evaluation specifically: an AI's 'no evidence found' must not be interpreted as 'no dependency exists'; argues AI systems must be evaluated on what they failed to discover, not only on what they extracted, calling this a fundamentally different evaluation problem.

rationale_evidence.anchor: Known gap: d \in D^*\setminus D_t ... Unknown gap: D^*\setminus D_t is itself partially unknown. That is the deepest form of Zero. ... Zero(K_t) may itself contain unresolved structure.
rationale_evidence.statement: Distinguishes a 'known gap' (a specific missing dimension d ∈ D*\D_t is identified) from an 'unknown gap' (D*\D_t is itself partially unknown, i.e. we don't know which dimensions are missing), and generalizes this to recursive uncertainty about unknown dimensions, unknown relationships, and unknown interpretations — concluding Zero(K_t) may itself contain unresolved structure and therefore should not be an ordinary database field.

rationale_evidence.anchor: Lord: Ω, the ideal knowledge/reality space. Zero: Ω-K_t ... Lord defines the horizon. Zero examines our inability to see the entire horizon.
rationale_evidence.statement: Describes Lord and Zero as near mathematically dual: Lord = Ω (the ideal space), Zero = Ω−K_t (the boundary, itself partially unknown since Ω is not fully enumerable); Lord defines the horizon, Zero examines the system's inability to see the entire horizon.

rows.statement: A prior claim that I-4 was falsified is retracted: a discharge summary is not authoritative because it was projected, but became authoritative through DERIVED -> REVIEWED -> ATTESTED -> RELEASED; governance created the authority, not the derivation. rows.anchor: The precise gap — located mechanically ... THE GAP: STATUS HAS A GOVERNED STATE MACHINE. AUTHORITY DOES NOT
rows.statement: statuses.yaml and authorities.yaml are declared orthogonal but are not equally equipped: statuses.yaml has 8 values, a progression field (order), a terminal marker (settled), a defined who-may-move role table, and lint-checkable transition guards; authorities.yaml has 5 values and none of these. Authority gates a status transition, but nothing governs how authority itself changes — no rule for who may move derived->authoritative, and no guard for it. This is exactly the I-4 problem: attestation is an authority transition (derived->authoritative); because authority transitions are ungoverned, the model cannot express 'attested', so it collapses derived into 'never authoritative'. A prior reviewer's diagnosis ('DP-2 conflates derivation and attestation') now has a mechanical cause.
