rows.anchor: The progression mechanisms — inventoried as evidence (P-1..P-10)
rows.statement: Ten progression mechanisms inventoried as observations, not assumed lifecycles: P-1 document status (8 values, order+settled+roles+guards); P-2 Authority (5 values with rank, no order/roles/guards); P-3 ES-006.1 promotion ladder; P-4 Methodology maturity; P-5 ADR-M status; P-6 Capability lifecycle; P-7 EEP (plan->...->decide); P-8 Observation Protocol (ACTIVE->CONCLUDED); P-9 Identifier lifecycles (4 series); P-10 Evidence accumulation (n=0->n=1->n>=2). A prior canonical distinction (Reference Model section 6, GEP-F1: two lifecycles never conflated, governance-artifact vs governed-work) is found before theorizing; this discovery extends that refusal rather than founding it.

rows.anchor: The flagship finding — authority is not one dimension ... authorities.yaml's own header asks TWO questions in ONE field: "how much should I trust this and where did it come from?"
rows.statement: authorities.yaml's five values answer two different questions: 'generated' and 'derived' answer provenance (where did it come from), and can never change (origin is an immutable historical fact); 'authoritative', 'provisional', and 'historical' answer standing (how much should I trust it), and can change by a governance act. This dissolves LG-1 ('should authority have a governed state machine?') rather than answering it: half of authority cannot have a state machine (provenance never changes) and the other half changes by governance acts recorded as act-logs, not workflows. Authority = an immutable PROVENANCE fact x a mutable STANDING judgment; attestation changes standing, nothing changes provenance. This also explains why the I-4 confusion was persistent: 'derived' (provenance) was wrongly read as entailing low standing, but a signed financial statement can be derived in provenance and authoritative in standing simultaneously.

rows.anchor: Invariant relationships vs implementation choices ... I-1..I-11 ... 11 invariants · 8 choices
rows.statement: Eleven invariants traced to governed statements: I-1 Knowledge is represented by an Artifact, an Artifact is never the Knowledge; I-2 a Capability protects exactly one invariant; I-3 a Knowledge Space has a declared boundary; I-4 (underspecified, not false — holds until attestation, reclassified as a lifecycle gap not an ontology falsification, per DP-2's conflation of derivation with attestation); I-5 one authoritative artifact per topic+context (lint-enforced); I-6 the Runtime never owns Knowledge; I-7 a PKS never contains reusable Method (stated and breached); I-8 governance precedes automation; I-9 governance-status orthogonal to authority; I-10 a constitutional principle is void-overriding; I-11 (restated 2026-08-02: Knowledge does not execute, capabilities execute, knowledge constrains and informs generation — the restatement survived cross-product projection where the original would have failed). Eight implementation choices (folder mapping, markdown as representation, YAML/Mermaid, the graph's declared scope, Claude Code as the n=1 runtime adapter, frontmatter, identifier formats, Mermaid+markdown projections) may change freely without breaking the model — that distinction is what makes this a platform rather than a repository layout.

rows.anchor: F-1 · I-4 — FALSIFICATION WITHDRAWN 2026-08-02 ... A projection CAN be authoritative. The invariant is true of the platform's own knowledge projections and FALSE as a general rule
rows.statement: I-4 ('a Projection is derived and cited as authority by nothing') is falsified as a general rule by counterexamples: a hospital discharge summary is generated from the record and legally authoritative (cited by clinician, insurer, court); a financial statement is generated from the ledger, then signed and filed, cited by auditors as authority. It holds only for PublicDigit's own projections (graph, portal indexes, cited by nothing). This is later reconciled (a self-correction within this same document): I-4 is not false but underspecified — it holds until attestation; DP-2 conflates derivation with authority; the mechanical cause is that authorities.yaml has no governed state machine so 'attested' cannot be expressed. Diagnosis: derived describes provenance, authoritative describes standing, and a signed derivation can be both.

rows.anchor: W3C PROV defines provenance as information about entities, activities, agents ... Provenance is frequently treated as: governance information, trust information, domain information ... simultaneously. Not purely infrastructure metadata.
rows.statement: W3C PROV (2013) defines provenance via primitives Entity/Activity/Agent/Derivation/Attribution; research finds provenance is simultaneously governance information, trust information, and domain information, and should not be treated as purely infrastructure metadata.

rows.anchor: Knowledge validity and recording time are different concepts ... 'What was considered authoritative at time T?' ... requires temporal state, authority state, lineage state simultaneously.
rows.statement: Temporal-database research treats knowledge validity and recording time as different concepts, recurring across valid time, transaction time, observation time, decision time, and effective time; the key research question is 'What was considered authoritative at time T?', which requires temporal state, authority state, and lineage state simultaneously (bitemporal models specifically referenced).

rows.anchor: Authority is organizational, not epistemic. A proposition may be: well-supported, unauthorized, or: authorized, uncertain.
rows.statement: Knowledge-governance research repeatedly distinguishes Creation/Proposal/Validation/Approval/Publication/Supersession/Retirement as lifecycle stages, and holds that authority is organizational, not epistemic: a proposition may be well-supported but unauthorized, or authorized but uncertain -- research supports keeping these separate.

rows.anchor: PROV-DM Core Concepts: Entity, Activity, Agent, Generation, Usage, Communication, Attribution, Association, Delegation
rows.statement: Second-pass draft expands the PROV-DM primitive list beyond pass 1's five (Entity/Activity/Agent/Derivation/Attribution) to nine: Entity, Activity, Agent, Generation, Usage, Communication, Attribution, Association, Delegation; also adds industry practice that provenance is 'increasingly treated as a control layer, not window dressing', with four checks: source identity, source version, retrieval path, answer-to-source alignment.

rows.anchor: SOURCE PROVENANCE (who/when/where/version/source) ... EPISTEMIC PROVENANCE (why selected, how generated, under what conditions, what selection procedure, what alternatives excluded).
rows.statement: Evidence provenance is two-dimensional: Source Provenance (who/when/where/version) versus Acquisition/Epistemic Provenance (why selected, how generated, conditions, selection procedure, excluded alternatives), called a major architectural insight; KnowledgeOS SHALL treat selection procedure as epistemic provenance, not merely operational metadata.
invariants: KnowledgeOS SHALL treat selection procedure as epistemic provenance, not merely operational metadata.

rows.anchor: Provenance | not separated from lineage | Π, intrinsic | ABSENT (authority is trust, not origin) | CONTRADICTED — three objects share the word
rows.statement: Triangulation row 'Provenance': the corpus never separates provenance from lineage; mathematics models Pi as intrinsic; EKP has no provenance field (its 'authority' field records trust-rank, not origin); canonical conclusion CONTRADICTED — three distinct objects (provenance, lineage, authority-as-trust) share a single overloaded corpus word.

rows.anchor: D-3 · Provenance vs lineage. Origin: never separated in the corpus. Production code separates three objects. VERDICT: CONTRADICTED — the corpus is under-differentiated; a split is required.
rows.statement: D-3 disagreement traced: the corpus never separates provenance from lineage, but production code independently separates three distinct objects; VERDICT CONTRADICTED — the corpus's under-differentiation is judged wrong, and a formal split of provenance from lineage (and from authority-as-trust) is required.

rows.anchor: 'provenance must be preserved somewhere' does not entail Provenance⊆K. The four candidate placements must therefore be tested against the mandatory operations rather than selected by architectural preference.
rows.statement: Governing methodological framing: the requirement that provenance be preserved SOMEWHERE does not entail that it belongs inside the Knowledge State K — four candidate placements must be tested against mandatory operations rather than chosen by architectural preference.

rows.anchor: Π = origin of an assertion versus History(T) = sequence of transformations. The executed reconciliation explicitly says these are genuinely different. ... Before any KnowledgeOS transformation has occurred: History(T)=∅. Yet an assertion in K0 may have originated from a document; a measurement; an e
rows.statement: Provenance Pi (origin of an assertion) is distinguished from History(T) (sequence of transformations) and shown genuinely different via a base-case counterexample: the initial state K0 has an empty transformation history (History(T)=empty) yet its assertions can still have external origins (a document, measurement, external system, human statement) — so History(T)=empty does not imply Provenance=empty, refuting Provenance=History(T) as a universal identity in the general case.

rows.anchor: Candidate A: Π⊆K. Candidate B: Π⊆H. Candidate C: Π⊆ExternalAudit. Candidate D: Π⊆ExternalContext. The prompt requires each to be evaluated against: mandatory operations; deterministic access; persistence; merge/split; replay; equality; validation; explanation.
rows.statement: Four candidate placements for provenance are set up for systematic testing against eight criteria (mandatory operations, deterministic access, persistence, merge/split, replay, equality, validation, explanation): Pi inside K, Pi inside History, Pi inside an external audit system, and Pi treated as external context.

rows.anchor: Does provenance need to be part of the semantic identity of the current state, or does K merely need a stable reference to it? Those are different claims. ... Let π be a provenance reference. Let P_π be the actual provenance record/object. Then π∈K does not imply P_π∈K. This gives a potentially much
rows.statement: The key distinction driving the whole step: whether provenance must be part of K's semantic identity, versus whether K merely needs a stable REFERENCE to it, are different claims; a provenance reference pi is distinguished from the full provenance record/object P_pi (mirroring an established EvidenceReference != EvidenceObject principle), so pi being in K does not imply P_pi is in K — yielding a potentially much smaller kernel.

rows.anchor: Π=History(T)? No — not universally. The base-case counterexample disproves this. ... REFUTED as a universal identity. But a weaker statement survives: History(T) can reconstruct internal transformation lineage. It cannot replace external provenance. ... external audit alone is insufficient unless K
rows.statement: Candidates B, C, and D are each addressed: Candidate B (Pi=History(T)) is REFUTED as a universal identity by the base-case counterexample, though History(T) can still reconstruct internal transformation lineage; Candidate C (external-audit-only) is found insufficient alone because Merge could destroy the provenance association unless K itself carries a stable resolvable reference, pushing back toward pi in K; Candidate D (provenance-as-context) is refuted because context ('under what circumstances does this apply') and provenance ('where did this originate') answer different questions and are already kept as distinct fields.

rows.anchor: Know Sometimes ... Challenge Yes, often ... Preserve Yes provenance cannot disappear ... Merge Yes contributing origins must survive ... Split Yes derived fragments retain origin ... Replay Partly history handles transformations ... Explanation Yes reconstruct why assertion exists ... Equality Not n
rows.statement: A full mandatory-operation matrix (Know, Compare, Challenge, Update, Preserve, Merge, Split, Replay, Validation, Explanation, Equality) rates provenance's necessity per operation, concluding provenance is operationally required across most of them (especially Preserve, Merge, Split, Explanation) but that this operational necessity does not mean every operation must treat provenance as part of semantic equality — preventing provenance from being overloaded with identity semantics.

rows.anchor: Persist(K)⇒Persist(ProvenanceReference). It does not necessarily require Persist(K)⇒Persist(ProvenanceObject inside K). ... Merge preserves provenance association. The provenance objects themselves need not be copied into the merged state. ... provenance needs stable identity across transformations
rows.statement: Four operation-specific constraints are derived: persistence requires persisting the provenance REFERENCE, not necessarily the full object inside K; merge must preserve provenance association for both merged assertions without needing to copy the provenance objects themselves into the merged state; split must preserve the relationship from each derived fragment back to the origin of the whole; and replay requires the pair (initial provenance Pi_0, transformation history H), not history alone, exactly reflecting the base-case distinction.

rows.anchor: Provenance preservation does not imply provenance-sensitive semantic equality. This is a major architectural result. ... K stores sufficient provenance identity for deterministic resolution. The external provenance service may store the larger graph. ... explanation requires both Π and History(T). T
rows.statement: Major architectural result: preserving provenance does not imply that semantic equality must be provenance-sensitive (K1 equiv K2 can hold under semantic equality with different Pi, while K1 cong_Pi K2 differs) — the two equality notions from Step 261 must not be conflated; validation only needs K to store sufficient provenance identity for deterministic resolution (the external service can hold the larger graph); and explanation of 'why does KnowledgeOS believe this' requires both Pi and History(T) together, reinforcing Provenance != History as two complementary rather than substitutable paths.

rows.anchor: KNOWLEDGE STATE -> Assertion A -> Provenance Π (origin of A -> external source) and History H (transformations -> T1→T2→T3). The provenance branch answers: Where did this assertion originate? The history branch answers: How did this state evolve? The executed reconciliation explicitly describes thes
rows.statement: The 'two-lineage model' formalizes Assertion A as having two distinct, complementary (not competing) lineage branches: Provenance Pi answering 'where did this assertion originate' (leading to an external source) and History H answering 'how did this state evolve' (a chain of transformations T1->T2->T3).

rows.anchor: The evidence does not require FullProvenanceGraph⊆K. It requires ProvenanceReference⊆K if KnowledgeOS must preserve deterministic association between an assertion and its origin. The detailed provenance graph may remain external: ProvenanceObject⊆ExternalProvenanceStore while π∈K acts as its stable
rows.statement: Smallest-defensible-placement result: the evidence requires only ProvenanceReference subset-of K (not the full provenance graph), with the detailed ProvenanceObject kept in an external provenance store and the in-K reference pi acting as its stable anchor — a strictly smaller kernel than embedding the entire provenance graph.

rows.anchor: A=(id,P,e,c,t,π) where π∈𝒫ℐ is a provenance reference. Then ResolveProvenance: 𝒫ℐ → ProvenanceObject. And internal lineage is separately History(A)=(T1,T2,…,Tn). Thus ProvenanceReference≠History.
rows.statement: Proposed final architecture: Assertion A=(id,P,e,c,t,pi) where pi is a provenance reference drawn from a reference universe PI, resolved by a function ResolveProvenance:PI->ProvenanceObject, kept explicitly distinct from the separately-tracked internal transformation lineage History(A)=(T1,...,Tn).

rows.anchor: Persistence: π survives serialization. Merge preservation: Different provenance references survive merging. Replay: Initial origin survives independently of transformation history. Explanation: The reference resolves to the source graph. Equality flexibility: Semantic equality can ignore provenance
rows.statement: Seven reasons are given for preferring the reference-based architecture over embedding: it survives serialization, distinct provenance references survive merging, initial origin survives independently of transformation history under replay, explanations can resolve the reference to the full source graph on demand, semantic equality retains the flexibility to ignore provenance when appropriate, the kernel stays minimal (the external graph need not enter K), and it gives a clean DDD aggregate/reference boundary (the assertion owns the reference; a separate provenance subsystem owns the graph).

rows.anchor: We must not upgrade this immediately to a universal theorem. ... VERIFIED: provenance cannot universally be derived from History(T). ... DERIVED/RECOMMENDED: store a stable provenance reference in K. ... rather than: PROVEN: full provenance object belongs in K.
rows.statement: Explicit evidentiary-discipline caution against overclaiming: the step's actual epistemic status is VERIFIED that provenance cannot universally be derived from History(T), and DERIVED/RECOMMENDED that a stable provenance reference should be stored in K — carefully distinguished from the stronger, unearned claim that the full provenance object is PROVEN to belong in K; whether every KnowledgeOS deployment requires provenance as part of semantic state identity remains a separate, open question.

rows.anchor: Full provenance object in K 🟡 Possible, but not minimal ... Provenance reference in K 🟢 Strongest current placement ... Full provenance in H 🔴 Refuted — fails at t=0 ... Provenance only in external audit 🟡 Insufficient alone ... Provenance as context 🔴 Refuted — different semantic role ... Provenanc
rows.statement: Final placement matrix rates all seven considered candidates: full object in K (possible but not minimal), reference in K (strongest current placement), full provenance in History (refuted, fails at t=0), external-audit-only (insufficient alone), provenance-as-context (refuted), the combined external-object-plus-in-K-reference model (preferred), and internal lineage tracked in History (valid, since it is transformation-derived).

rows.anchor: PROVENANCE PLACEMENT: SUBSTANTIALLY RESOLVED. KnowledgeOS must preserve provenance association, but the evidence does not require the complete provenance object to be embedded in the Knowledge State. ... π∈K while ProvenanceObject⇏K and Provenance≠History(T). ... Provenance placement substantially r
rows.statement: Step 265 verdict: PROVENANCE PLACEMENT SUBSTANTIALLY RESOLVED — pi is in K while the full ProvenanceObject is not required to be, and Provenance remains distinct from History(T); this closes provenance placement in the research-band status table (alongside K representation, Assertion type, and Proposition type as 'largely/fully constrained'), setting up Step 266 to ask whether every currently claimed KnowledgeOS construct can actually be computed, decided, persisted, replayed and validated.

rows.anchor: Do not simply put provenance back into K. Investigate three possibilities: A Provenance is a component of knowledge state. B Provenance is an external relation: Provenance : Assertion → Source. C Lineage is a property of transformation history: Lineage = History(T). ... The external-source/t=0 count
rows.statement: Poses the exact three-candidate provenance-placement question (component of K / external relation / property of History) later resolved by this batch's Step 265, explicitly requiring the t=0 external-source counterexample to be handled — the precise counterexample Step 265 uses to refute Candidate B.

rows.anchor: StructuralEquality = COMPUTABLE under canonical representation. ... SemanticEquality = CONDITIONAL not universally established [3m/300cm needs unit normalization; conceptual entities may need an ontology/identity registry]. ... IdentityConstruction can be computable, while IdentityResolution may rem
rows.statement: Equality, identity, and provenance are each split into a computable mechanical half and a conditional/non-computable semantic half: structural equality is computable via canonicalization+hashing while semantic equality is only conditionally computable (domain-dependent, e.g. unit normalization for 3m vs 300cm); identity CONSTRUCTION (deterministic hashing of canonical data) is computable while identity RESOLUTION (whether two independently-supplied references denote the same real-world entity) may remain externally supplied or human-governed; provenance-reference LOOKUP is computable under three infrastructure assumptions, but this never establishes ProvenanceTruth — lookup is not validation.

rows.anchor: K₁ = δ(K₀, e₀) computed end-to-end, 28 of 30 symbols resolved · six K candidates constructed and scored · provenance models A/B/C against nine scenarios (A: 8/9, B: 3/9, C: 3/9) · policy composition laws · policy equality (four notions) · Σ ten-case audit · the corpus's own ladder_dc_reference.py ex
rows.statement: Executed-computation baseline entries not previously recorded in this exact form: a concrete state transition K1=delta(K0,e0) was computed end to end resolving 28 of 30 required symbols; six distinct K candidates were constructed and scored; three provenance-placement models (A, B, C) were tested against nine scenarios with A scoring 8/9 and both B and C scoring only 3/9 each, giving Candidate A (provenance inside the assertion/state) a decisive empirical edge.

rows.statement: Implementation-evidence baseline records a THIRD distinct provenance-related object beyond Provenance and Lineage: EventProvenance, alongside ReplayAssertion (content-hash identity, immutable) and EvidenceSet (holds no transport, per ADR-T16) as separate real implementation artifacts.

rows.anchor: Model B fails on merge and dedup because it puts Π outside the content that determines id.
rows.statement: A precise mechanical reason Provenance-as-external-map (Candidate B) fails merge and deduplication: it places Pi outside the content used to compute an assertion's content-addressed id, so the id computation cannot see or preserve the provenance association during those operations.

rows.anchor: typed provenance graph implemented, empirically supported. ... Provenance infrastructure = EMPIRICALLY SUPPORTED. But the key question is: Assertion.Π ↔ ImplementationProvenanceReference. We cannot claim the full mapping until the assertion implementation exists. ... Provenance subsystem exists, but
rows.statement: Provenance infrastructure (a typed provenance graph) is empirically supported, but the canonical correspondence between an Assertion's Pi field and the implementation's provenance reference cannot be closed until the Assertion object itself is implemented — the provenance subsystem existing is not sufficient on its own.

rows.anchor: Π AssertionOrigin | where the claim came from; intrinsic; t=0-safe | in Assertion ... EvidenceProvenance | chain of custody of one evidence item | in Evidence (230.15) ... History(T) | ordered record of system transformations; starts at t=0 | external to K ... MessageProvenance | (correlationId, cau
rows.statement: Provenance is resolved into FOUR distinct objects, not the three previously known: AssertionOrigin (Pi, intrinsic, t=0-safe), EvidenceProvenance (chain of custody of one evidence item, per corpus step 230.15), History(T) (system transformation record, starts at t=0), and a newly surfaced fourth object, MessageProvenance ((correlationId, causationId), belonging to Integration Events in another bounded context) — four objects, four names, no shared word.

rows.anchor: Epistemology/Semantics → Measurable structure → Measurement ... the kernel preserves substrate, not derived mathematics: KOS_core=(Identity, Participants, Context, Boundary, Time, Observations, Relations, Provenance, History, Transitions, AccessScope, RegimeReferences) ... Measure theory becomes one
rows.statement: The repaired ARC-A model (established 2026-08-25 ~19:00) externalizes measure theory entirely: the kernel preserves only a domain-agnostic substrate (KOS_core, a twelve-field tuple including Provenance, History, Transitions, RegimeReferences), with probabilistic, logical, causal, statistical and other regimes all treated as pluggable, non-foundational add-ons.

rows.anchor: Both states hold the SAME two propositions with the SAME per-assertion provenance. They differ ONLY in whether a derivation relation exists. ... withdraw('vendor'): KA -> [...] KB -> [...] ... OBSERVED: the two states agree on every proposition AND on every proposition's provenance, yet withdraw() d
rows.statement: EXP-2 is the decisive result of the file: two states KA and KB, agreeing on every proposition AND every proposition's per-assertion provenance (identical Pi values), differing only in whether a 'derives' relation exists between two assertions, are still distinguished by the withdraw() operation — proving that provenance placed INSIDE the assertion (Step 265's placement verdict) is NOT the component that restores sufficiency; the load-bearing component is instead the relation set R (specifically R_der). This directly qualifies Step 265's provenance-placement conclusion as orthogonal to the sufficiency question it is usually cited to have resolved.

experiment.hypothesis: H2: placing provenance inside the assertion (rather than in K=(A,R) alone) restores sufficiency
experiment.setup: KA and KB share identical assertions a1,b1 with identical per-assertion provenance; KA additionally has a 'derives' relation between them, KB has none
experiment.assumptions: content-only equality (eq_content) as the candidate abstraction; OPS_FULL as the tested operation set
experiment.inputs: two K instances differing only in R
experiment.method: check eq_content(KA,KB); compare op_withdraw_source results for both
experiment.result: content-only equality says equal; withdraw('vendor') produces different resulting states for KA vs KB
experiment.interpretation: the distinguishing information lived in R (the derives relation), not in Pi (which was identical in both) -- provenance-in-the-assertion did not do the sufficiency work
experiment.limitations: single constructed pair; only the withdraw operation exercised the difference
experiment.conclusion: H2 as usually stated is misattributed: sufficiency for this case comes from R, not from Pi's placement

rationale_evidence.anchor: The reviewer proposes a "Provenance Domain" ... Verdict: PROVENANCE is not a missing domain — it is a DISPERSED, NAMED, PARTLY-GOVERNED concern
rationale_evidence.statement: A check-before-recording pass finds provenance already lives in the corpus as: one axis of AUTHORITY itself (provenance x standing, Engineering Progression Model, PM-1), the PROVENANCE non-progression kind, identity discipline (CAP-001), evidence grading practice ([FETCHED]/[CANONICAL]/[2nd-hand]), and append-only evidence/traceability blocks. Verdict: provenance is a dispersed, named, partly-governed concern (the SP-5 pattern recognized a third time), not a missing domain. Disposition: the provenance questions enrich the existing Tier-1 Knowledge Governance stream (PM-1); 'Provenance as a strategic domain' is recorded as a hypothesis routed to the docket, admissible only if a live stream produces evidence requiring it; the identity-chain observation (CAP-001 as foundation if provenance grows) is a watch item, not a promotion.

rationale_evidence.anchor: The precise gap — located mechanically ... THE GAP: STATUS HAS A GOVERNED STATE MACHINE. AUTHORITY DOES NOT
rationale_evidence.statement: statuses.yaml and authorities.yaml are declared orthogonal but are not equally equipped: statuses.yaml has 8 values, a progression field (order), a terminal marker (settled), a defined who-may-move role table, and lint-checkable transition guards; authorities.yaml has 5 values and none of these. Authority gates a status transition, but nothing governs how authority itself changes — no rule for who may move derived->authoritative, and no guard for it. This is exactly the I-4 problem: attestation is an authority transition (derived->authoritative); because authority transitions are ungoverned, the model cannot express 'attested', so it collapses derived into 'never authoritative'. A prior reviewer's diagnosis ('DP-2 conflates derivation and attestation') now has a mechanical cause.

rationale_evidence.anchor: The four concerns, separated as required ... A fifth concern the repository already separates ... TRUST/PROVENANCE = authorities.yaml
rationale_evidence.statement: Four concerns mapped to dimensions: EVIDENCE (D-V, new), GOVERNANCE (D-III, existing/executable via statuses.yaml), OPERATIONAL STATE (D-VI, new), INTENT (derived: f(GOVERNANCE-STATUS, OWNER), both fields already exist). A fifth concern the repository already separates, worth naming so it is not re-added later: TRUST/PROVENANCE = authorities.yaml (authoritative, derived, generated, historical, provisional), and statuses.yaml already declares status independent of authority — the repository was doing orthogonal dimensions before this commission asked for them.

rationale_evidence.anchor: The progression mechanisms — inventoried as evidence (P-1..P-10)
rationale_evidence.statement: Ten progression mechanisms inventoried as observations, not assumed lifecycles: P-1 document status (8 values, order+settled+roles+guards); P-2 Authority (5 values with rank, no order/roles/guards); P-3 ES-006.1 promotion ladder; P-4 Methodology maturity; P-5 ADR-M status; P-6 Capability lifecycle; P-7 EEP (plan->...->decide); P-8 Observation Protocol (ACTIVE->CONCLUDED); P-9 Identifier lifecycles (4 series); P-10 Evidence accumulation (n=0->n=1->n>=2). A prior canonical distinction (Reference Model section 6, GEP-F1: two lifecycles never conflated, governance-artifact vs governed-work) is found before theorizing; this discovery extends that refusal rather than founding it.

rationale_evidence.anchor: W3C PROV defines provenance as information about entities, activities, agents ... Provenance is frequently treated as: governance information, trust information, domain information ... simultaneously. Not purely infrastructure metadata.
rationale_evidence.statement: W3C PROV (2013) defines provenance via primitives Entity/Activity/Agent/Derivation/Attribution; research finds provenance is simultaneously governance information, trust information, and domain information, and should not be treated as purely infrastructure metadata.

rationale_evidence.anchor: Knowledge validity and recording time are different concepts ... 'What was considered authoritative at time T?' ... requires temporal state, authority state, lineage state simultaneously.
rationale_evidence.statement: Temporal-database research treats knowledge validity and recording time as different concepts, recurring across valid time, transaction time, observation time, decision time, and effective time; the key research question is 'What was considered authoritative at time T?', which requires temporal state, authority state, and lineage state simultaneously (bitemporal models specifically referenced).

rationale_evidence.anchor: Provenance | not separated from lineage | Π, intrinsic | ABSENT (authority is trust, not origin) | CONTRADICTED — three objects share the word
rationale_evidence.statement: Triangulation row 'Provenance': the corpus never separates provenance from lineage; mathematics models Pi as intrinsic; EKP has no provenance field (its 'authority' field records trust-rank, not origin); canonical conclusion CONTRADICTED — three distinct objects (provenance, lineage, authority-as-trust) share a single overloaded corpus word.

rationale_evidence.anchor: D-3 · Provenance vs lineage. Origin: never separated in the corpus. Production code separates three objects. VERDICT: CONTRADICTED — the corpus is under-differentiated; a split is required.
rationale_evidence.statement: D-3 disagreement traced: the corpus never separates provenance from lineage, but production code independently separates three distinct objects; VERDICT CONTRADICTED — the corpus's under-differentiation is judged wrong, and a formal split of provenance from lineage (and from authority-as-trust) is required.

rationale_evidence.anchor: Π=History(T)? No — not universally. The base-case counterexample disproves this. ... REFUTED as a universal identity. But a weaker statement survives: History(T) can reconstruct internal transformation lineage. It cannot replace external provenance. ... external audit alone is insufficient unless K
rationale_evidence.statement: Candidates B, C, and D are each addressed: Candidate B (Pi=History(T)) is REFUTED as a universal identity by the base-case counterexample, though History(T) can still reconstruct internal transformation lineage; Candidate C (external-audit-only) is found insufficient alone because Merge could destroy the provenance association unless K itself carries a stable resolvable reference, pushing back toward pi in K; Candidate D (provenance-as-context) is refuted because context ('under what circumstances does this apply') and provenance ('where did this originate') answer different questions and are already kept as distinct fields.

rationale_evidence.anchor: Provenance preservation does not imply provenance-sensitive semantic equality. This is a major architectural result. ... K stores sufficient provenance identity for deterministic resolution. The external provenance service may store the larger graph. ... explanation requires both Π and History(T). T
rationale_evidence.statement: Major architectural result: preserving provenance does not imply that semantic equality must be provenance-sensitive (K1 equiv K2 can hold under semantic equality with different Pi, while K1 cong_Pi K2 differs) — the two equality notions from Step 261 must not be conflated; validation only needs K to store sufficient provenance identity for deterministic resolution (the external service can hold the larger graph); and explanation of 'why does KnowledgeOS believe this' requires both Pi and History(T) together, reinforcing Provenance != History as two complementary rather than substitutable paths.

rationale_evidence.anchor: Persistence: π survives serialization. Merge preservation: Different provenance references survive merging. Replay: Initial origin survives independently of transformation history. Explanation: The reference resolves to the source graph. Equality flexibility: Semantic equality can ignore provenance
rationale_evidence.statement: Seven reasons are given for preferring the reference-based architecture over embedding: it survives serialization, distinct provenance references survive merging, initial origin survives independently of transformation history under replay, explanations can resolve the reference to the full source graph on demand, semantic equality retains the flexibility to ignore provenance when appropriate, the kernel stays minimal (the external graph need not enter K), and it gives a clean DDD aggregate/reference boundary (the assertion owns the reference; a separate provenance subsystem owns the graph).

rationale_evidence.anchor: Model B fails on merge and dedup because it puts Π outside the content that determines id.
rationale_evidence.statement: A precise mechanical reason Provenance-as-external-map (Candidate B) fails merge and deduplication: it places Pi outside the content used to compute an assertion's content-addressed id, so the id computation cannot see or preserve the provenance association during those operations.

rows.anchor: Status: APPROVED WITH STRUCTURAL CORRECTIONS / Authority: HPA Supervisory
rows.statement: HPA Supervisory issues a formal ruling approving the revised complete TODO register for KnowledgeOS Theory v1.2, with structural corrections applied to the prior dependency structure.

rows.anchor: 1. **Factivity does NOT block Contr** — Contradiction semantics can be investigated independently
rows.statement: Corrects a prior (implicit) dependency assumption: Factivity does not block Contr; contradiction semantics can be investigated independently of the factivity decision.

rows.anchor: 2. **Composition separated from Reduction** — Different research concerns
rows.statement: Composition (how evaluation results/transitions/structures combine) is corrected to be a separate research concern from Reduction (minimizing representation while preserving invariants), not a sub-step of it.

rows.anchor: 3. **Projection/Invariant as parallel foundational lane** — Not dependent on δ
rows.statement: The Projection/Invariant framework is corrected to be a parallel foundational research lane, not dependent on δ (state transition) being defined first.

rows.anchor: 4. **≡sem as candidate prerequisite, not established foundation**
rows.statement: Semantic equivalence (≡sem) is downgraded from an established foundation to merely a candidate prerequisite for certain forms of kernel reduction; FR-001 established it is not refuted, but its sufficiency for reduction has not been shown.

rows.anchor: 5. **Kernel selection depends on what proves load-bearing, not mechanically on every TODO A–H**
rows.statement: Kernel selection is corrected to depend only on whichever subset of TODO groups A-I is demonstrated to be semantically load-bearing, not mechanically on completion of every group.

rows.anchor: | **DECISION** | Conceptual choice required | Factivity, ⪰ |
rows.statement: Defines six TODO types used to classify all open KnowledgeOS work items: DECISION (conceptual choice), EXPERIMENT (empirical/mathematical test), DEFINITION (formal semantics missing), REDUCTION (determine kernel-essentiality), GOVERNANCE (ratification/adoption), RESEARCH (foundational investigation).

rows.anchor: > **Does KnowledgeOS claim truth, or only epistemic warrant?**
rows.statement: TODO Group A (Factivity): does KnowledgeOS claim truth, or only epistemic warrant? Sub-todos: define 'knowledge' without truth in its domain (A1), decide factivity (A2), locate factivity as mathematical property/external assumption/architectural boundary/not-required (A3), choose among Rename/Externalize/Hybrid (A4).

rows.anchor: The v1.1 witness established that \(K_t = \Gamma(E_t, Q, C, EC)\) cannot simultaneously be an attributive knowledge construction and be factive if truth is absent from Γ's domain.
rows.statement: Restates the v1.1 witness finding: K_t=Γ(E_t,Q,C,EC) cannot be simultaneously an attributive construction and factive when truth is absent from Γ's domain; two possible worlds with identical epistemic input but different truth values produce the same epistemic state.

rows.anchor: | **Externalize** | Factivity is verified outside the kernel; kernel emits claims | 88.25% survival rate measurable (under tested conditions) |
rows.statement: Three factivity-resolution candidates: Rename (A_t=Attributed State, 'Knows' external — honest but weaker), Externalize (factivity verified outside kernel; 88.25% survival rate measured under tested conditions — an experimental result, not an architectural recommendation), Hybrid (some attributed states factive, some not — most complex/expressive).

rows.anchor: > **Can contradiction be represented without confusing it with uncertainty, absence, insufficient evidence, or theory incompleteness?**
rows.statement: TODO Group B (Contr), status OPEN — NEXT EXPERIMENT, does not depend on Factivity: can contradiction be represented without confusing it with uncertainty, absence, insufficient evidence, or theory incompleteness? Sub-todos B1-B4: run the contradiction experiment against four candidates, define Contr semantics, define Zero under contradiction, resolve minimum evaluation domain (C may or may not emerge).

rows.anchor: `Sat_content` is not a function on contradictory states. Both \(p \in K\) and \(\neg p \in K\) can hold simultaneously. The current codomain `{T, F, U}` cannot represent this.
rows.statement: Sat_content is not a well-defined function on contradictory states: both p∈K and ¬p∈K can hold simultaneously, and the current three-value codomain {T,F,U} cannot represent this.

rows.anchor: | **Structured Evaluation** | `EVal = (value, reason, provenance)` | Most expressive; keeps contradiction distinct |
rows.statement: Four candidate resolutions for the contradiction/evaluation-domain problem: Fourth Value (add C to codomain, changes whole evaluation algebra), Delegate to Consistency (Sat_content returns U on contradiction, makes content depend on a blocked class), Exclusive by Construction (⊥≡(¬p∈K∧p∉K), silently loses the contradiction), Structured Evaluation (EVal=(value,reason,provenance), most expressive, keeps contradiction distinct).

rows.anchor: > **Determine the minimum evaluation domain required** — then `C` may emerge, or may not. Do not let the simulator force the theory to supply a value merely because the simulator needs one.
rows.statement: States a methodological principle guarding against a specific failure mode: determine the minimum evaluation domain required for contradiction semantics first; do not let implementation/simulator needs force the theory to manufacture a value it does not independently require.

rows.anchor: > **How does KnowledgeOS order epistemic progress?**
rows.statement: TODO Group C (⪰, progress ordering): how does KnowledgeOS order epistemic progress? 1,491 claims specify no ordering; progress is meaningless without one. Sub-todos C1-C5: define what is ordered, define x⪰y explicitly, determine order type (preorder/partial/total/preference/dominance/admissibility), keep admissibility≠ranking≠selection explicit, allow multiple orderings (accuracy/coverage/decision/robustness).

rows.anchor: > There may be **no universal total ordering**. Progress may be multi-dimensional.
rows.statement: Hypothesizes that there may be no universal total ordering of epistemic progress in KnowledgeOS; progress may instead be irreducibly multi-dimensional.

rows.anchor: The Linga-Yoni experiment showed that generation ≠ progress. A system can change without improving.
rows.statement: Restates a finding attributed to the (prior-batch) Linga-Yoni experiment: generation is not progress — a system can change state without that change constituting improvement, motivating the need for an explicit progress ordering.

rows.anchor: > **What exactly does semantic equivalence mean in KnowledgeOS?**
rows.statement: TODO Group D (≡sem): what exactly does semantic equivalence mean? Sub-todos D1-D8: define semantic contract/scope, identity scope, context sensitivity, temporal sensitivity, provenance relevance, distinguish observational/semantic/operational equivalence, determine decidability, define relation to object identity.

rows.anchor: > Semantic equivalence is a candidate prerequisite for certain forms of kernel reduction. Equivalence + required invariants + observability + adequacy + operational preservation may all be needed.
rows.statement: States that reduction plausibly requires more than semantic equivalence alone: equivalence + required invariants + observability + adequacy + operational preservation may all be jointly necessary (this same composite requirement recurs verbatim under TODO Group I).

rows.anchor: > **What are the exact semantics of state transition?**
rows.statement: TODO Group E (δ, state transition): what are the exact semantics of δ? Sub-todos E1-E4: define the signature δ(K,o,Γ)→K', define transition causes (observation/determination/decision/action/revision/retraction/supersession), define transition composition, define closure semantics (ClosureEvent≠ClosureState).

rows.anchor: **δ does not block static semantics. δ blocks composition and dynamics.**
rows.statement: Distinguishes that the undefined transition function δ blocks composition and dynamics specifically, but does not block investigation of static epistemic semantics.

rows.anchor: > **What is the lifecycle of a knowledge claim?**
rows.statement: TODO Group F (Lifecycle/Retirement): what is the lifecycle of a knowledge claim? Sub-todos F1-F5: define retirement, retraction, supersession, expiration, and lifecycle relations — explicitly investigating relations/events rather than assuming a state machine.

rows.anchor: > Lifecycle should investigate **relations/events**, not automatically create a state machine. ClosureEvent ≠ ClosureState.
rows.statement: Restates (from the prior Epistemic Closure Event track) that lifecycle/retirement should be modeled via relations/events rather than assumed to require a state machine, reaffirming ClosureEvent≠ClosureState.

rows.anchor: > **How do evaluation results / transitions / structures combine?**
rows.statement: TODO Group G (Composition): how do evaluation results, transitions, and structures combine? Sub-todos G1-G3: define evaluation composition, transition composition, and structure composition, as a concern separate from Reduction.

rows.anchor: | **H1** | Define the framework | Structure → Projection → Induced Equivalence → Information Loss → Invariant Preservation → Adequacy |
rows.statement: Restates the structure-first Projection/Invariant framework pipeline (Structure → Projection → Induced Equivalence → Information Loss → Invariant Preservation → Adequacy) as TODO Group H, marked [PROP]/RESEARCH, possibly the mathematical foundation of the whole kernel.

rows.anchor: > **How can representation be minimized while preserving required distinctions/invariants?**
rows.statement: TODO Group I (Reduction): how can representation be minimized while preserving required distinctions/invariants? Depends on ≡sem, Composition, and the Invariant framework; sub-todos I1-I4 define reduction criteria, apply the Adequacy Principle, identify invariant-bearing distinctions, and determine whether a minimal rich structure actually exists.

rows.anchor: | **1** | **B — Contr** | Immediate next experiment | EXPERIMENT |
rows.statement: Sets the revised priority order for the ten TODO groups: 1-Contr (immediate next experiment), 2-Factivity, 3-⪰, 4-Projection/Invariant, 5-≡sem, 6-δ, 7-Lifecycle, 8-Composition, 9-Reduction, 10-Kernel Selection.

rows.anchor: | **Continue N_eff formula hunt** | FR-001 closes the formula hunt |
rows.statement: Enumerates seven explicit prohibitions for the current phase: do not continue the N_eff formula hunt (FR-001 closes it), do not make Factivity block Contr, do not make Yoni/Linga architecture, do not make Gita concepts primitives (v1.2 constitutional separation intact), do not implement the eight Sat classes (semantics not closed), do not select the kernel yet, do not create Theory v1.3 yet.

rows.anchor: **Next: B — Contradiction / Evaluation Domain / Zero Experiment**
rows.statement: HPA ruling designates the Contradiction/Evaluation-Domain/Zero experiment as the mandated next research action.

rows.anchor: Yes — **I agree with the attached TODO register in its overall structure and intent**, but I would **not approve it unchanged**.
rows.statement: Agrees with the TODO register's overall structure/intent but refuses unchanged approval, objecting specifically to the linearity of its dependency graph.

rows.anchor: From the experiments we have actually run, **contradiction semantics can be investigated independently of the final factivity decision**.
rows.statement: Argues, citing already-run experiments, that Factivity->Contr is not a justified dependency: contradiction semantics (p,¬p∈K) can be investigated without deciding whether p is true in the world.
Cites an already-established result (Truth ⊥ Closure) as grounds for decoupling Factivity from Contr in the dependency graph.

rows.anchor: I would **not put the 88.25% survival rate into the candidate architecture decision unless that percentage is explicitly tied to a particular experiment and scope**.
rows.statement: Warns against letting the 88.25% survival-rate experimental result be read as an architectural recommendation for the Externalize factivity option unless explicitly scoped to its originating experiment.

rows.anchor:
I would make one important methodological addition:

### Do NOT make the experiment's purpose “choose C or no C.”
rows.statement: Adds a methodological constraint on the Contr experiment: its purpose should be to determine the minimum evaluation domain required, not to prematurely choose whether a fourth value C exists.

rows.anchor: You can define what the relation *purports* to order before knowing all its eventual semantics.
rows.statement: Argues ⪰ (progress ordering) need not wait for Factivity and Contr to be fully closed: what the relation purports to order can be defined before its full semantics are settled.

rows.statement: Justifies downgrading ≡sem from 'foundation of kernel reduction' to 'candidate prerequisite': projection research has not shown equivalence alone suffices; equivalence+invariants+observability+adequacy+operational preservation are jointly needed.

rows.anchor: That's fair as a **research statement**, but don't let it imply that static epistemic semantics cannot be studied before δ.
rows.statement: Distinguishes that although 'without transition semantics the entire dynamics is undefined' is a fair research statement, it must not be read as blocking study of static epistemic semantics before δ is defined.

The title combines:

> **Composition/Reduction**

but these are actually different questions.

rows.anchor: So lifecycle should investigate **relations/events**, not automatically create a state machine.
rows.statement: Restates ClosureEvent≠ClosureState as grounds for requiring lifecycle/retirement to be modeled as relations/events rather than assumed to be a state machine.

rows.anchor: But the projection/invariant programme is conceptually relevant to **how you evaluate D, E, F, and kernel reduction**.

to:

rows.anchor:
Currently the document sometimes mixes:

### A. Semantic questions
... ### B. Research questions
... ### C. Architectural decisions
rows.statement: Distinguishes three kinds of TODO being conflated in the register: semantic questions (what does contradiction mean?), research questions (does structure-first survive adversarial testing?), and architectural decisions (what belongs in the kernel?) — motivating the DECISION/EXPERIMENT/DEFINITION/REDUCTION/GOVERNANCE typing scheme.

rows.anchor: Yes. **I agree with this revised register substantially, and I would now treat it as a sound active research roadmap.**
rows.statement: A reviewer agrees substantially with the revised TODO register (S2478/S2483 body) and would treat it as a sound active research roadmap, confirming all nine corrected points (Factivity/Contr independence, Contr as next experiment, parallel ⪰ analysis with admissibility≠ranking≠selection, ≡sem as candidate prerequisite, δ/Lifecycle separation, Projection/Invariant as parallel lane, Composition/Reduction separation, kernel selection depending on load-bearing subset, N_eff off critical path).

rows.anchor: The **diagram currently places Reduction before δ, Lifecycle and Composition**, while the text says Reduction depends on Composition and the invariant framework... That is inconsistent.
rows.statement: Flags one remaining internal inconsistency in the register: its dependency diagram places Reduction before delta/Lifecycle/Composition, while its own text states Reduction depends on Composition and the Invariant framework; supplies a corrected diagram routing delta/Lifecycle into Composition into Reduction.

rows.anchor: Even that should be understood as a **dependency map, not necessarily a mandatory execution sequence**.
rows.statement: Warns that even the corrected dependency diagram should be read as a dependency map, not a mandatory execution sequence.

rows.anchor:
**[APPROVED] with one diagram/dependency consistency correction.**

The important thing is that the register has now moved from a **linear TODO list** toward a **research dependency graph**.
rows.statement: Issues the final governance verdict: [APPROVED] with one diagram/dependency-consistency correction; notes the register's most important structural achievement is moving from a linear TODO list to a research dependency graph, appropriate to the programme's current semantic-definition/evaluation gate (not a kernel-selection gate).

rows.anchor: KnowledgeOS may have many pieces of evidence supporting incompatible propositions. How does it determine what may be accepted, what remains uncertain, what is rejected, and what must be escalated? The answer should not be "choose the most trustworthy source." We need to separate authority, evidentia
rows.statement: Frames Step 19's central problem: choosing among conflicting evidence must not reduce to 'pick the most trustworthy source' — authority, evidential support, reliability, applicability, independence, and epistemic commitment must be kept separate.

rows.anchor:
The fundamental distinction ... Evidence 
eq Truth and Source 
eq Evidence ... Authority 
eq Reliability and Reliability 
eq Evidential Support and Evidential Support 
eq Knowledge Commitment. These are different properties.
rows.statement: States five separated properties: Evidence≠Truth, Source≠Evidence, Authority≠Reliability, Reliability≠EvidentialSupport, EvidentialSupport≠KnowledgeCommitment.

rows.anchor: Why this matters ... Source A An official constitution ... Source B An engineer says ... Source C An LLM says ... KnowledgeOS cannot simply calculate (1+1+1)/3. This is not a democracy. Knowledge commitment is governed epistemic synthesis, not source voting.
rows.statement: Illustrates with a constitution/engineer/LLM three-source example that KnowledgeOS cannot average opinions — 'Knowledge commitment is governed epistemic synthesis, not source voting.'

rows.anchor: Source ... S=(SourceID,Type,Origin,Owner,Context,AuthorityProfile,ReliabilityProfile,TemporalScope,Provenance). A source is a producer/container of information. It is not itself evidence for every proposition it contains. ... Source versus evidence ... Source \supset Evidence conceptually. A source
rows.statement: Defines Source=(SourceID,Type,Origin,Owner,Context,AuthorityProfile,ReliabilityProfile,TemporalScope,Provenance) as distinct from Evidence — a source is not itself evidence for every proposition it contains (Source ⊃ Evidence).

rows.anchor: Evidence support ... Support(e,A) = (Direction,Strength,Specificity,Directness,Completeness) ... Direction = supports / contradicts / neutral; Strength = how strongly; Specificity = how directly it addresses A; Directness = direct observation versus inference; Completeness = whether relevant informa
rows.statement: Defines a structured five-dimension Support(e,A)=(Direction,Strength,Specificity,Directness,Completeness) instead of a scalar.

rows.anchor: Authority ... Who or what has the legitimate right to establish a proposition or rule in this context? ... Constitution Very high for governance rules ... LLM No intrinsic organizational authority ... Authority(S,A,Ctx) must be contextual. ... Authority is not universal ... an architecture board doe
rows.statement: Defines contextual Authority(S,A,Ctx) (worked with a seven-source authority table), establishing Authority is scoped — high authority in one domain does not transfer to another.

rows.anchor: Reliability ... How consistently does this source produce information that turns out to correspond to the relevant domain state? Rel(S,A,Ctx,t) can be estimated from historical performance. ... Reliability is empirical ... \hat p=990/1000=0.99. But we should not immediately declare Reliability=0.99.
rows.statement: Defines empirically-estimated Reliability Rel(S,A,Ctx,t), warning a raw hit-rate must account for sampling/independence/bias/measurement-error/confidence-intervals — Reliability is an estimate, not an intrinsic metaphysical property.

rows.anchor: Statistical reliability ... \hat p=k/n ... p\sim Beta(\alpha,\beta) and after k successes in n observations p\mid data \sim Beta(\alpha+k,\beta+n-k). This gives KnowledgeOS a principled way to represent source reliability uncertainty.
rows.statement: Defines a Bayesian Beta-Binomial estimator for source reliability p|data~Beta(α+k,β+n-k), representing reliability uncertainty as a distribution rather than a point estimate.

rows.anchor: But source reliability is not proposition reliability ... Rel(S,Infrastructure)=High but Rel(S,LegalInterpretation)=Low. Reliability(S)\neq Reliability(S,A). This is an important correction to simplistic trust scores.
rows.statement: Corrects simplistic single-value trust scores: Reliability(S) ≠ Reliability(S,A) — a source can be reliable in one domain and unreliable in another.

rows.anchor: Applicability ... Applicable(S,A,Ctx,t) ... A 2024 architecture decision may be authoritative, but no longer applicable after a 2026 superseding decision. Authority \land Reliability does not imply Applicability. ... Temporal validity ... T_v(S,A) must be considered. Commitment = f(Authority,Support
rows.statement: Defines Applicable(S,A,Ctx,t) as a third dimension distinct from Authority and Reliability — Authority∧Reliability does not imply Applicability, especially once superseded — feeding Commitment=f(Authority,Support,Reliability,Applicability,Time,...).

rows.anchor: Independence ... five websites repeat ... suppose all five copied the same original article. n=5 does not mean five independent observations. Independence(e_i,e_j) or at least an estimate of dependence. ... Evidence correlation ... EffectiveEvidence(e_1,e_2,e_3)<3. This prevents evidence inflation.
rows.statement: Reaffirms that apparent multi-source agreement (five websites) can collapse to one effective observation if all derive from a common original, requiring an explicit evidence-dependency graph — Corroboration depends on independence, not merely source count.

rows.anchor: Contradictory evidence ... e_1\Rightarrow A and e_2\Rightarrow \neg A. We should not immediately calculate A=0.5. Instead create EvidenceConflict(A,\neg A). Then evaluate authority; reliability; applicability; time; independence; specificity; directness.
rows.statement: Requires contradictory evidence produce an explicit EvidenceConflict(A,¬A) object evaluated across seven dimensions, rather than collapsing to a naive average like A=0.5.

rows.anchor: Evidence comparison ... W(e,A,C)=(Authority,Reliability,Directness,Specificity,Freshness,Independence,Completeness). This is a profile, not necessarily a single number. ... Why not simply create one evidence score? Because dimensions can conflict. Old Constitution: Very high authority, Low directnes
rows.statement: Defines the seven-dimension evidence comparison profile W(e,A,C), warning against collapsing to one score since dimensions can conflict (e.g. an old authoritative constitution vs a fresh but lower-authority database state) — Evidence comparison is purpose and proposition dependent.

rows.anchor: Evidence ordering ... e_1\succeq e_2 if w_i(e_1)\geq w_i(e_2) for all relevant i. This gives us a Pareto-style evidence ordering. ... Evidence need not be totally ordered ... e_1\nsucceq e_2 and e_2\nsucceq e_1. They are incomparable under the current ordering. EvidenceComparison=Incomparable rather
rows.statement: Defines a Pareto-style partial order over evidence (e1⪰e2), explicitly allowing evidence to be mutually Incomparable rather than forcing a winner.

rows.anchor: Source authority hierarchy ... Constitution > Policy > Procedure > Guideline > Recommendation. But this hierarchy must itself be a governed rule. It is not a universal law of KnowledgeOS. AuthorityHierarchy is domain policy. ... Proposition-specific authority ... Authority(ArchitectureBoard,Architec
rows.statement: Requires any source-authority hierarchy (e.g. Constitution>Policy>Procedure>Guideline>Recommendation) itself be a governed policy, not a universal law, since a single global trust ranking would be absurd across unrelated proposition types.

rows.anchor: Source reliability matrix ... R_{S,A,C} ... CMDB High infrastructure, Low architecture, None business policy ... LLM Candidate only across all. This is far more useful than Trust(LLM)=0.6.
rows.statement: Proposes a source×assertion-type×context reliability matrix (worked with a five-source example) as far more useful than a single scalar trust score.

rows.anchor: LLMs require special treatment ... LLMOutput be modeled as a generated informational artifact, not as a trusted source of organizational truth. Authority(LLM,GovernanceRule)=0 unless the organization explicitly assigns authority. Its outputs become CandidateEvidence or CandidateAssertion or Candidat
rows.statement: Requires LLM output be modeled as a generated informational artifact with Authority(LLM,GovernanceRule)=0 by default, entering only as Candidate — LLM→Candidate→EvidenceAssessment→GovernedKnowledge, never LLM→Truth, a defining KnowledgeOS architectural property.

rows.anchor: Knowledge commitment ... Candidate \rightarrow Supported \rightarrow Corroborated \rightarrow Accepted \rightarrow Committed. But this is not necessarily a universal linear lifecycle. Candidate\rightarrow Rejected. Candidate\rightarrow Undetermined. Supported\rightarrow Superseded.
rows.statement: Defines a five-stage Knowledge Commitment lifecycle (Candidate→Supported→Corroborated→Accepted→Committed) with explicit non-linear branches (to Rejected, Undetermined, Superseded).

rows.anchor: What does "committed" mean? ... A proposition is knowledge-committed when the system is authorized to use it as an accepted premise within a specified context and purpose. Committed_\rho(A,K,Ctx,t) means: Under governance policy \rho, assertion A is admitted into the committed knowledge state for co
rows.statement: Defines Committed_ρ(A,K,Ctx,t) as policy-relative admission into the committed knowledge state, purpose- and context-sensitive rather than universal.

rows.anchor: Knowledge state partition ... K=K_C\cup K_S\cup K_U\cup K_X where K_C committed knowledge; K_S supported but not committed; K_U unresolved/uncertain; K_X rejected/superseded historical knowledge. This prevents the database from collapsing everything into one truth bucket. ... Committed knowledge is
rows.statement: Partitions K into K_committed∪K_supported∪K_uncertain∪K_historical, and states Committed(A) ⇏ universally true — only that KnowledgeOS is permitted to treat A as accepted knowledge given its epistemic and governance state.

rows.anchor: Commitment function ... Commit_\rho(A,K,E) \rightarrow Status where Status\in\{Commit,Reject,Defer,Escalate,RemainUncertain\}. The function considers Evidence, Authority, Reliability, Applicability, TemporalValidity, Independence, Conflict, Purpose, Governance. ... A structured commitment predicate
rows.statement: Defines Commit_ρ(A,K,E)→{Commit,Reject,Defer,Escalate,RemainUncertain} as a conjunctive structural predicate (Eligible∧Supported∧Applicable∧Governed∧TemporalValid∧¬UnresolvedCriticalConflict), explicitly better than a bare threshold score like Score(A)>0.7.

rows.anchor: Thresholds ... Support(A)\geq0.8. But we should distinguish Threshold from Truth. A threshold is a governance decision. Thresholds are policy, not mathematics of truth.
rows.statement: States a numeric acceptance threshold is a governance decision, not mathematics of truth — Thresholds are policy.

rows.anchor: Bayesian reasoning ... P(A\mid E) = P(E\mid A)P(A)/P(E) can be used when its assumptions are appropriate. But P(A\mid E)=0.95 does not automatically imply Committed(A). The commitment threshold is governed separately. ... Why probability cannot replace commitment ... P(FirewallRuleCorrect)=0.99. If
rows.statement: States a high Bayesian posterior P(A|E)=0.95 does not automatically imply Committed(A); EpistemicProbability ≠ OperationalPermission, since catastrophic-if-wrong actions may still require human verification even at 0.99.

rows.anchor: Evidence aggregation ... P(E_1,\ldots,E_n\mid A) = \prod_iP(E_i\mid A) under conditional independence. But that assumption is often false. Therefore KnowledgeOS should record Dependency(E_i,E_j). ... No naive evidence multiplication ... E_2=Copy(E_1) then P(E_1,E_2\mid A) must not be treated as P(E_
rows.statement: Warns against naively multiplying likelihoods across correlated evidence (e.g. a copied record) — a major statistical safeguard requiring explicit Dependency(Ei,Ej) tracking.

rows.anchor: Reliability learning ... n predictions and k correct outcomes. p\sim Beta(\alpha,\beta). After observations p\mid D\sim Beta(\alpha+k,\beta+n-k). The result is not merely Source trusted = 0.83. Instead SourceReliabilityEstimate = Distribution which preserves uncertainty. ... Source reliability can d
rows.statement: Represents source reliability as a full Beta-updated distribution rather than a point estimate, and states both Reliability and Authority are temporal/non-stationary, connecting to Step 16's versioning.

rows.anchor: Source quality versus evidence quality ... Quality(Source) from Quality(Evidence). A reliable database has a stale record. SourceQuality=High but EvidenceQuality=Low. This distinction will prevent many false conclusions.
rows.statement: Distinguishes Quality(Source) from Quality(Evidence), illustrated by a generally reliable database holding one stale record — high source quality does not guarantee high quality for a particular piece of evidence.

rows.anchor: Conclusion synthesis ... Assertion: A ... Supporting: E1,E2,E3 ... Contradicting: E4 ... Independence: E1/E2 dependent, E3 independent ... Status: Supported but disputed. This is vastly more informative than A=0.73. ... The conclusion object ... KnowledgeAssessment KA=(Assertion,SupportingEvidence,C
rows.statement: Defines a structured KnowledgeAssessment object KA (eleven fields) as the bridge between Evidence and Knowledge State, far more informative than a bare scalar like A=0.73.

rows.anchor: The Knowledge Commitment lifecycle ... Observed → Extracted → Assessed → Supported → Corroborated/Disputed → Commitment Decision → Committed / Rejected / Deferred / Escalated / Uncertain. Notice that Disputed does not automatically mean Rejected. ... Commitment can be revoked ... Committed(A) \right
rows.statement: Defines the full Knowledge Commitment lifecycle (Observed→Extracted→Assessed→Supported→Corroborated/Disputed→Commitment Decision) with Disputed≠Rejected, revocability (Committed→UnderReview→Retracted), and a KnowledgeCommitted domain event recording why an assertion became committed.

rows.anchor: Human commitment ... This architecture decision is approved. The LLM cannot commit that. The Architecture Board can. CommitmentAuthority must be explicit. ... Automated commitment ... Monitoring reports CPU = 91.2%. If the monitoring system is the system of record and the proposition is within its a
rows.statement: Requires explicit CommitmentAuthority: some propositions require human authorization (architecture approvals) while others (system-of-record telemetry) may be safely auto-committed under AutomationPermission(A,Ctx) policy.

rows.anchor: This produces a beautiful distinction ... Evidence \rightarrow Assessment \rightarrow Commitment ... Authority controls who/what may commit. while Reliability controls how much evidential trust we place. These are fundamentally different dimensions.
rows.statement: Draws the summary distinction: Authority controls who/what may commit, while Reliability controls how much evidential trust to place — fundamentally different dimensions.

rows.anchor: Evidence weighting is therefore not a single formula ... I would explicitly reject the naive model W=w_1A+w_2R+w_3F. It can be useful as an approximation in controlled situations, but it should not be the fundamental KnowledgeOS model. The fundamental model should be EvidenceProfile = (A,R,S,D,F,I,C
rows.statement: Explicitly rejects a linear-weighted-sum evidence formula W=w1A+w2R+w3F as the fundamental model (though usable as a policy approximation), requiring instead a structured non-collapsed EvidenceProfile.

rows.anchor: The general commitment function ... Commit_\rho(A,E,S,Ctx,t,P) \rightarrow \mathcal S where \mathcal S=\{Committed,Supported,Disputed,Uncertain,Rejected,Deferred,Escalated\}.
rows.statement: Consolidates the general commitment function Commit_ρ(A,E,S,Ctx,t,P)→S over seven-valued output {Committed,Supported,Disputed,Uncertain,Rejected,Deferred,Escalated}.

rows.anchor: Knowledge State after Step 19 ... K_t=(K_t^{committed},K_t^{supported},K_t^{uncertain},K_t^{disputed},K_t^{historical}). This is a much more powerful model than K_t=\{facts\}. ... Knowledge commitment is not binary ... Candidate, Supported, Corroborated, Disputed, Uncertain, Committed, Rejected, Sup
rows.statement: Refines K_t into a five-part partition (committed/supported/uncertain/disputed/historical) and an eight-value epistemic-status vocabulary, far richer than a flat fact set.

rows.anchor: The complete evidence-to-knowledge pipeline ... Source \rightarrow Evidence \rightarrow EvidenceAssessment \rightarrow AssertionAssessment \rightarrow CommitmentDecision \rightarrow KnowledgeState with Authority + Reliability + Applicability + TemporalValidity + Independence + Conflict acting as eva
rows.statement: Assembles the complete evidence-to-knowledge pipeline (Source→Evidence→EvidenceAssessment→AssertionAssessment→CommitmentDecision→KnowledgeState) with six cross-cutting evaluation dimensions.

rows.anchor: Connection to Zero ... InsufficientEvidence, AuthorityConflict, ReliabilityConcern, SourceDependence, TemporalExpiry, UnresolvedConflict, UncommittedCriticalKnowledge. Thus a discrepancy is not simply "Something is missing." It may be "We have information, but it is not sufficiently authorized or re
rows.statement: Extends Zero to detect seven authority/reliability/independence-based discrepancy types, showing a deficiency can mean 'insufficiently authorized to commit' not merely 'missing', and extends Lord to six evidence-improving actions.

rows.anchor: Connection to Sārathi ... Is the evidence sufficient to act? Supported(A) may be enough for InformationalAnswer. But not enough for ProductionChange. RequiredEvidenceLevel depends on action risk. This is a major connection between Steps 15 and 19. ... Risk-adjusted epistemic requirement ... Required
rows.statement: Formally connects Step 19 to Step 15's decision theory: RequiredConfidence=f(Risk,Impact,Reversibility,Purpose) — epistemic requirements increase with consequence, so the same evidence level may suffice for informational answers but not production changes.

rows.anchor: KnowledgeOS can therefore answer different classes of questions ... Informational: Supported + Committed. Decision support: CommittedCriticalKnowledge + RiskAssessment. Governance: Authority + ApplicablePolicy + DecisionGovernance. Execution: Authorization + ExecutionCapability. These are distinct c
rows.statement: Classifies four distinct question-answering capabilities (Informational, Decision support, Governance, Execution) each requiring a different composition of Step 19's machinery.

rows.anchor:
Step 19 invariants ... A1 Source
eq Evidence ... A2 Authority

eq EvidentialSupport ... A4 EvidentialSupport

rows.statement: States fifteen candidate invariants A1-A15 covering Source/Authority/Reliability/EvidentialSupport/KnowledgeCommitment separation, contextual/temporal authority and reliability, evidence-count vs independent corroboration, contradiction preservation, policy-governed (not metaphysical) commitment, no intrinsic LLM authority, purpose-dependent commitment, probability vs operational permission, risk-scaled evidence requirements, and reversible/traceable commitment.

rows.anchor: Step 19 mathematical core ... E=(Source,Observation,Content,Support,Provenance,TemporalScope) ... SA(S,A,C,t)=(Authority,Reliability,Applicability,Freshness) ... EA(E,A,C)=(Support,Directness,Specificity,Independence,Completeness) ... AA(A,E,S,C,t,P) ... Commit_\rho(A,\cdots) \rightarrow CommitmentS
rows.statement: Consolidates the Step 19 mathematical core: evidence structure E, source assessment SA, evidence assessment EA, assertion assessment AA, and the commitment function.

rows.anchor: The most important result of Step 19 ... How does KnowledgeOS decide what information is allowed to become governed knowledge? Not by LLM confidence. Not by number of sources. Not by one trust score. Instead: Knowledge Commitment = Evidence Assessment + Authority + Reliability + Applicability + Temp
rows.statement: States the central Step 19 result: Knowledge Commitment is the sum of eight preserved dimensions (Evidence Assessment, Authority, Reliability, Applicability, Temporal Validity, Independence, Conflict Handling, Governance Policy) — never LLM confidence, source count, or a single trust score.

rows.anchor: Step 19 verdict ... THEORETICALLY RESOLVED AT THE FRAMEWORK LEVEL ... we have defined the semantics, but we have deliberately not yet fixed universal numerical formulas for authority, reliability, or evidence aggregation. That is not a weakness. It is correct architecture. Those quantities are often
rows.statement: Declares Step 19 theoretically resolved at the framework level, deliberately leaving numerical formulas for authority/reliability/aggregation domain- and policy-dependent rather than fixed, called correct architecture, not weakness.

rows.anchor: Where we are now ... Sources \rightarrow Evidence \rightarrow Assessment \rightarrow Commitment \rightarrow Knowledge \rightarrow Semantic Interpretation \rightarrow Zero \rightarrow Discrepancy \rightarrow Lord \rightarrow CandidateActions \rightarrow Sārathi \rightarrow Decision \rightarrow Govern
rows.statement: Assembles the cumulative pipeline through Step 19 (Sources→Evidence→Assessment→Commitment→Knowledge→Zero/Lord/Sārathi→Decision→GovernedAction→Event→Observation) with eight cross-cutting dimensions, declared closer to a formal epistemic operating architecture than a conventional AI knowledge base.

rows.anchor: The next step I recommend ... we have not yet formally defined uncertainty itself across the different kinds of uncertainty we encounter. rows.statement: Poses Step 20: formally distinguish six uncertainty kinds (Unknown/Ambiguous/Probabilistic/Conflicting/Incomplete/Imprecise), noting an LLM's stated confidence cannot be equated with a calibrated probability, to determine which uncertainty representations are computable versus requiring the system to honestly return Unknown/Undetermined.
